quote: (Judges 5:17) Gad remained beyond the Jordan. And this is set forth as a reproach because while Reuben remained, Gad remained with him of equal mind. And Dan was free with ships. For seeing that the tribes of Reuben and Gad did not go with their brothers to battle, being terrified by fear, he took flight by being free with ships. Asher dwelt on the seashore and stayed in the ports. Likewise, this is set forth as a reproach because Asher, while dwelling on the seashore, stayed in the ports, choosing instead to flee rather than fight with his brothers.
source_title: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

author: Jerome
quote: (Judges 5:18) Zebulun and Naphtali offered their lives unto death in the region of Morome. In Hebrew, it is 'super regionem Morome'. The meaning is that while the other tribes were unwilling to go, these two tribes offered their lives unto death. In the region of Morome. For Morome is interpreted as 'exalted': they are said to have offered their lives for the sake of the exalted region, that is, for God, and therefore they are praised, while the other tribes are criticized.
source_title: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

author: Jerome
quote: (Judges 5:19) Kings came and fought. The kings of the land of Canaan said, who were subject to King Jabin. The kings of Canaan fought. It repeats the same thing in Tanach. Tanach is indeed a province where the Kishon River is. Near the waters of Megiddo. Megiddo is a city situated on the Kishon River. And what is said, Near the waters of Megiddo, is understood near the Kishon River, the city of Megiddo. Yet they took nothing as plunderers. This is said in mocking, implying that not only did they not obtain any spoils, but they were also unable to save their own lives.
source_title: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

author: Jerome
quote: (Judges 5:20) There was a battle fought against them from heaven. Because in the forty thousand men of Israel a shield and spear could not be found, therefore the Lord fought for them from heaven with hailstones and fire against their enemies. Just as it is also written in the book of Joshua: The stars remained in their order and fought against Sisera (Joshua 10:11). The stars are understood to be the angels who fought against Sisera from heaven.
source_title: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

author: Jerome
quote: (Judges 5:21) The River Kishon swept away their corpses. For there is the place of their downfall; and it is as if one were to ask, where? and the answer is: In the River Kishon, that is, in the Red Sea. Hence it follows: The river Kishon, the river of Kishon. It calls the River Kishon the Red Sea. For Kishon means of old, because ancient miracles were performed there, when the children of Israel passed over and the Egyptians perished. And because the Red Sea vomited forth the dead Egyptians, so that the Israelites saw their dead bodies on the shore of the sea, and the same bodies were carried away by the fish and sea creatures: therefore the River Kishon swept away their corpses, so that the fish and sea creatures of the Red Sea might eat the bodies of the Canaanites, in place of the bodies of the Egyptians taken from them. Trample, my soul, the mighty ones. This is what Deborah, representing all of Israel, says, that they may crush the necks of their strongest enemies with one mind, that is, the strongest ones: as it is also written in the book of Joshua about the five kings of the Canaanites (Josh. 10:24).
source_title: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

author: Jerome
quote: (Judges 5:22) Then the hooves of the horses fell off, with a powerful force to those fleeing, and headlong to the bravest of the enemies who were rushing. 'Their hooves,' it is read in Hebrew; for it is reported that the hooves of their horses fell off from hailstones from the heavens, that is, from their angels. So the meaning is: If the hooves of the horses fell off from touching the stones, what do you think happened to the riders?
source_title: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

author: Jerome
quote: (Judges 5:23) Cursed be the land of Meroz, said the Angel of the Lord. In Hebrew it is written: Curse Meroz, said the Angel of the Lord. The Angel of the Lord is understood by the Hebrews to be Michael, who commands Deborah to have the people of Israel curse Meroz, that is, the power of the Angel that presided over the Canaanites. For Meroz is interpreted as secret. Therefore, he is commanded to be cursed, that is, anathematized, because while the other angels fought for Israel, he not only did not fight, but also persevered in their adversity. Curse the inhabitants of Meroz, says the Lord's angel. Curse them bitterly because they did not come to help the Lord. They did not come to help the strong Lord.
source_title: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

author: Jerome
quote: (Judges 5:24) Blessed among women, Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite. Among women, namely Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Leah, and almost all women. Let her be blessed in the temple, the Lord is understood, so that her memorial may be there, just like Judith. And the reason why she is blessed is given, namely because she acted wisely and prudently, in that she gave milk to the one asking for water. Therefore, she gave milk, so that the fleeing enemy would find a stronger faith in her. And if it is asked why he did not give wine, it must be answered that the house of Rechab do not drink wine, as you have in the prophet Jeremiah (Jer. XXXV, 14).
source_title: Commentary on the Song of Deborah

author: Jerome
quote: The truth of the Lord reaches even to the clouds. The clouds are the apostles and prophets; to them he gave the command not to rain upon Israel. This is in agreement with history as recorded in the book of Judges, where it speaks of the fleece that was dry while rain fell upon the rest of the world. It means that Israel is dry and the rain is pouring down over the whole world.

author: Jerome
quote: They who were glorying in their army, whose king was the Assyrian and who used to boast "I will scale the heavens," not only fell down to earth but on the ground became dung."Make their nobles." What nobles? Those who fight against your people. "Like Oreb and Zeeb; all their chiefs like Zebah and Zalmunna." I suppose you have read in the book of Judges the story of Gideon, who is also called Jerubbaal, how he outwitted those four kings while fighting for the people of God and put an end to them. And notice the kind of nobles these Midianites are who abandoned the judgment of God: "Oreb and Zeeb; all their chiefs like Zebah and Zalmunna." Who would dream that such words contain mysteries of the Savior? The philosophers read them and smile; the rhetoricians read them and sneer. Not only the rhetoricians, however, but the Jews, too; they have not the key to their treasures, for a veil covers their eyes. "Oreb" means a "hole in which a snake lurks"; "Zeeb" equals "wolf." Mark, now, the names of the chiefs of Christ's opponents: "Zebah," "victim or spoil that the wolf will strangle"; and "Zalmunna," "masters of malice." See, then, the divine secrets hidden away in names?

author: Jerome
quote: And whereas he [Jovinianus] prefers the fidelity of the father Jephthah to the tears of the virgin daughter, that corroborates our point. For we are not commending virgins of the world so much as those who are virgins for Christ's sake. Most Hebrews blame the father for the rash vow he made, "If you will indeed deliver the children of Ammon into my hand, then it shall be that whatsoever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me, when I return in peace from the children of Ammon, it shall be for the Lord's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering." Supposing (the Hebrews say) a dog or an ass had met him, what would he have done? Their meaning is that God so ordered events that he who had improvidently made a vow should learn his error by the death of his daughter.

author: Jerome
quote: At Gibeah also, now a complete ruin, she stopped for a little while remembering its sin, and the cutting of the concubine into pieces, and how in spite of all this three hundred men of the tribe of Benjamin were saved that in after days Paul might be called a Benjamite.

author: John Cassian
quote: Divine grace ever stirs up the will of human beings, not so as to protect and defend it in all things in such a way as to cause it not to fight by its own efforts against its spiritual adversaries, the victor over whom may set it down to God's grace, and the vanquished to his own weakness, and thus learn that his hope is always not in his own courage but in the divine assistance and that he must ever fly to his Protector. And to prove this not by our own conjecture but by still clearer passages of holy Scripture let us consider what we read in Joshua the son of Nun: "The Lord," it says, "left these nations and would not destroy them, that by them he might test Israel, whether they would keep the commandments of the Lord their God, and that they might learn to fight with their enemies." And if we may illustrate the incomparable mercy of our Creator from something earthly, not as being equal in kindness but as an illustration of mercy: if a tender and anxious nurse carries an infant in her bosom for a long time in order sometime to teach it to walk, and first allows it to crawl, then supports it that by the aid of her right hand it may lean on its alternate steps, presently leaves it for a little and if she sees it tottering at all, catches hold of it and grabs at it when falling, when down picks it up, and either shields it from a fall or allows it to fall lightly, and sets it up again after a tumble, but when she has brought it up to boyhood or the strength of youth or early manhood, lays upon it some burdens or labors by which it may be not overwhelmed but exercised, and allows it to vie with those of its own age; how much more does the heavenly Father of all know whom to carry in the bosom of his grace, whom to train to virtue in his sight by the exercise of free will, and yet he helps him in his efforts, hears him when he calls, leaves him not when he seeks him, and sometimes snatches him from peril even without his knowing it.

author: John Cassian
quote: As useful as it is to me that you [the Lord] should leave me for a little while in order to test the steadfastness of my desire, so it is harmful if you let me be abandoned for too long because of my deserts and my sins. For no human strength will be able to endure by its own steadfastness if it is too long abandoned by your help in time of trial. Nor will it be able to give way instantly before the power and wherewithal of the adversary if you yourself, who are aware of human strengths and are the arbiter of our struggles, "do not permit us to be tried beyond our capacity, but with the trial also provide a way out, so that we may be able to endure."We read something like this as it appears in mystical fashion in the book of Judges with respect to the extermination of the spiritual nations that are opposed to Israel: "These are the nations that the Lord forsook, so that by them he might instruct Israel, so that they might grow accustomed to fighting with their enemies." And again, a little further on: "The Lord left them so that he might test Israel with them, whether or not they would hear the commandments of the Lord that he had laid down for their forefathers by the hand of Moses." God did not begrudge Israel their peace or look with malice upon them, but he planned this conflict in the knowledge that it would be beneficial. Thus, constantly oppressed by the onslaught of the nations, they would never feel that they did not need the Lord's help. Hence they would always meditate on him and cry out to him, and they would neither lapse into sluggish inactivity nor lose their ability to fight and their training in virtue. For frequently security and prosperity have brought low those whom adversities cannot overcome.

author: John Cassian
quote: We frequently find this calling from need in Scripture as well, when we read that on account of their sins, the children of Israel were delivered over by the Lord to their enemies and that, having changed their course because of their domination and savage cruelty, they cried out to the Lord. "And the Lord sent them," it says, "a deliverer named Ehud, the son of Gera, the son of Jemini, who used either hand as if it were his right hand." And again it says, "They cried out to the Lord, who raised up a deliverer for them, Othniel, the son of Kenaz, the younger brother of Caleb, and he freed them." And it said of them in a psalm: "When he killed them, then they sought him, and they turned and at dawn they came to God, and they remembered that God was their helper." And again: "They cried out to the Lord when they were troubled, and he freed them from their distress."Of these three kinds [of calling from need], then, although the first two seem to be supported by better beginnings, nonetheless we find that even on the third level [recorded by the psalmist], which seems inferior and lukewarm, there have been people who are perfect and very fervent in spirit, similar to those who have made an excellent beginning in the Lord's service and have passed the rest of their lives in praiseworthy intensity of spirit. Likewise there are many who have become tepid and have fallen from a higher level and very frequently ended up in tragedy. [Thus], just as it was no drawback to the former that they seem to have been converted not by their own will but by force of necessity, inasmuch as the Lord's kindness furnished the occasion whereby they might feel compunction, likewise their having been converted in some sublime fashion profited the latter nothing whatsoever, because they did not strive to live out the rest of their days accordingly.

author: John Cassian
quote: These are the persons, then, who are referred to in holy Scripture as amphoterodexioi—that is, as ambidextrous. Ehud, "who used either hand as if it were his right hand," is described as such in the book of Judges. We shall also be able to possess this quality in a spiritual way if by a good and correct use we put the things which are considered fortunate and right-handed and the things which are called unfortunate and left-handed on the right side, that whatever befalls may become for us, in the words of the apostle, "the arms of righteousness." For we see that our inner man consists in two parts or, as I might say, two hands. No holy person can be without what we call the left hand, but perfect virtue is discerned in the fact that by proper use he turns both into a right hand.

author: John Chrysostom
quote: For nothing, nothing is more powerful than a pious and sensible woman to bring a man into proper order, and to mould his soul as she will. For he will not endure friends, or teachers, or rulers, as he will his partner advising and counseling him, since the advice carries even some pleasure with it, because she who gives the counsel is greatly loved. I could tell of many hard and disobedient men who have been softened in this way. For she who shares his table, his bed, and his embraces, his words and secrets, his comings in and goings out, and many other things, who is entirely given up and joined to him, as it is likely that a body would be joined to a head, if she happen to be discreet and well attuned, will go beyond and excel all others in the management of her husband. Wherefore I exhort women to make this their employment, and to give fitting counsel. For as they have great power for good, so have they also for evil. A woman destroyed Absalom, a woman destroyed Amnon, a woman was like to have destroyed Job, a woman rescued Nabal from the slaughter. Women have preserved whole nations; for Deborah and Judith exhibited successes worthy of men; so also do ten thousand other women. Wherefore Paul saith, "For what knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shall save thy husband?" And in those times we see Persis and Mary and Priscilla taking part in the labors of the Apostles; whom we also needs must imitate, and not by words only, but also by actions, bring into order him that dwelleth with us.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 61

author: John Chrysostom
quote: For Jephthah likewise, when he had promised that the first thing that met him, after a victorious battle, he would sacrifice, fell into the snare of child-murder; for his daughter first meeting him, he sacrificed her and God did not forbid it. And I know, indeed, that many of the unbelievers impugn us of cruelty and inhumanity on account of this sacrifice; but I should say, that the concession in the case of this sacrifice was a striking example of providence and clemency; and that it was in care for our race that He did not prevent that sacrifice. For if after that vow and promise He had forbidden the sacrifice, many also who were subsequent to Jephthah, in the expectation that God would not receive their vows, would have increased the number of such vows, and proceeding on their way would have fallen into child-murder. But now, by suffering this vow to be actually fulfilled, He put a stop to all such cases in future. And to shew that this is true, after Jephthah's daughter had been slain, in order that the calamity might be always remembered, and that her fate might not be consigned to oblivion, it became a law among the Jews, that the virgins assembling at the same season should bewail during forty days the sacrifice which had taken place; in order that renewing the memory of it by lamentation, they should make all men wiser for the future; and that they might learn that it was not after the mind of God that this should be done, for in that case He would not have permitted the virgins to bewail and lament her. And that what I have said is not conjectural, the event demonstrated; for after this sacrifice, no one vowed such a vow unto God. Therefore also He did not indeed forbid this; but what He had expressly enjoined in the case of Isaac, that He directly prohibited; plainly shewing through both cases, that He doth not delight in such sacrifices.

author: John Damascene
quote: In the relics of the saints the Lord Christ has provided us with saving fountains which in many ways pour out benefactions and gush with fragrant ointment. And let no one disbelieve. For, if by the will of God water poured out of the precipitous living rock in the desert, and for the thirsty Samson from the jawbone of an ass, is it unbelievable that fragrant ointment should flow from the relics of the martyrs? Certainly not, at least for such as know the power of God and the honor which the saints have from him.

author: Maximus of Turin
quote: Rightly, then, do we compare Mary with fleece—she who conceived the Lord in such a way that she absorbed him with her whole body; nor did she undergo a rending of that same body, but she was tender in submission and firm in chastity. Rightly, I say, is Mary compared with fleece—she from whose offspring saving garments are woven for the people. Clearly Mary is fleece since from her tender womb came forth the Lamb who himself, bearing his mother's wool (that is, flesh), covers the wounds of all peoples with a soft fleece. For every wound of sin is covered with the wool of Christ, tended by the blood of Christ, and, so that it may receive health, clothed in the garment of Christ.

author: Maximus of Turin
quote: Let us avoid, then, brothers, let us avoid the pestilential deceits of the insidious foxes [heretics]. Let us avoid the deadly frauds of wicked persons lest, like the foxes which that famous strong man Samson once sent into the Philistines' fields, bearing torches on their tails that burned up everything with their flames, the foxes of perverse teachings in like manner either get hold of the fruits of our fields by deceitful traps or consume them by burning flames. Let us, therefore, as we read, be simple and clever—that is to say, simple as doves and clever as serpents, so that the cleverness of the serpents might protect the simplicity of the doves.

author: Methodius of Olympus
quote: But lest I should appear to some to be sophistical, and to conjecture these things from mere probabilities, and to babble, I will bring forward to you, O virgins, from the Old Testament, written prophecy from the book of Judges, to show that I speak the truth, where the future reign of chastity was already clearly foretold.…Now it is clear that these things are not said of trees growing out of the earth. Inanimate trees cannot be assembled in council to choose a king since they are firmly fixed to the earth by deep roots. But on the whole these things are narrated concerning souls that—before the incarnation of Christ—luxuriated too deeply in transgressions, who approach God as beggars asking for mercy so that they may be governed by his pity and compassion. This mercy is what Scripture expresses by the figure of the olive, because oil is of great advantage to our bodies: it takes away our fatigue and ailments and offers light. For all lamplight increases when nourished by oil. So also God's mercies entirely dispel death, assist the human race and nourish the light of the heart. Consider the laws [which were in effect] from the first created man successively on to Christ. Weren't they imaginatively set forth in these words by the Scripture, in opposition to which the devil has deceived humanity? In it the fig tree has been associated with the command given to the man in paradise, because, when he was deceived, he covered his nakedness with the leaves of a fig tree; and the vine [has been related] to the instruction given to Noah at the time of the deluge, because he was mocked when overpowered by wine. The olive signifies the law given to Moses in the desert, because the prophetic grace, the holy oil, had failed from their inheritance when they broke the law. Lastly, the bramble aptly refers to the law that was given to the apostles for the salvation of the world: by their instruction we have been taught virginity, which is the only figure that the devil has not been able to make into a deceptive image. For this reason, also, the four Gospels have been given, because God has four times given the gospel to the human race and has instructed them by four laws, the times of which are clearly known by the diversity of the fruits. For the fig tree, on account of its sweetness and richness, represents the delights of man, which he had in paradise before the fall. Indeed, as we shall afterwards show, the Holy Spirit frequently takes the fruit of the fig tree as an emblem of goodness. But the vine, on account of the gladness produced by wine and the joy of those who were saved from wrath and from the deluge, signifies the change produced from fear and anxiety into joy. Moreover, the olive, on account of the oil that it produces, indicates the compassion of God, who again, after the deluge, bore patiently when people turned aside to ungodliness, so that he gave them the law and manifested himself to some, and nourished by oil the light of virtue, which is now almost extinguished.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
The reader of the present lesson was reading it thus: "and the people feared the Lord all the days of Joshua", but we have: "and the people served the Lord all the days of Joshua, and all the days of their elders, who were of longer days after Joshua". We must therefore understand that each one of us secures it for himself, whether he be in good days or in evil, and whether he have "the days of Joshua" — that is, the days of the righteous — or have the days of the impious. For if we understand "the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world", and offer it our souls to enlighten, or if "the sun of righteousness" rise upon us and "enlighten the world" of our soul, then we too have "the days of Jesus" Christ, the days of salvation. But if anyone offers his soul to receive that light which "shall be extinguished", the light contrary to the truth, and is enlightened by it, he too shall have days, but evil ones, and he will not be among the days of Joshua, but will be among the days of Manasseh, or among the days of Pharaoh, or among the days of some other most wicked man. Therefore, in short, in the days of Ahaz, that iniquitous and most wicked king, Isaiah could not see a vision, could not "see the Lord of Sabaoth seated upon a throne high and lifted up". But from the time that the wicked king died, whose were "the evil days", then the prophet could see the vision of God. And do you wish to know that these days, when they are spoken of in the scriptures as belonging to this man or that, do not signify the span of the life of the one who is spoken of, or of his bodily presence? Hear what the prophet foretold concerning the days of our Lord Jesus Christ: "there shall arise", he says, "in his days righteousness and abundance of peace, until the moon be taken away". If we take this thus, that "in the days" in which the Savior tarried on earth there were days "of righteousness" and days "of peace", how shall we prove that days "of righteousness" arose for those who crucified him and who did not receive his coming and the faith? Or how will "the abundance of peace in his days" be seen to have been among those who delivered him to death by false accusations? How to these will "days of righteousness and" days "of peace" be seen to have arisen, in whose minds the darkness of iniquity and of fury was at work? And again, if this which is written — "there shall arise in his days righteousness and abundance of peace" — be referred to those days which the Savior spent in the flesh, then now, since those days are not present, therefore "his righteousness does not arise" nor is the "abundance" of Christ's "peace" found among the faithful and the religious. Rather, then, each one according to his own acts and manner of life acquires for himself "days" either of iniquity and of war, or "of righteousness" and "of peace". Hear, in short, the prophet saying: "to those who fear my name", he says, "shall the sun of righteousness arise", doubtless that it may make for them "days of righteousness", "days of Jesus". But of the impious he says that "the sun of righteousness" will set for them — doubtless for those in whom righteousness sleeps, and for whom the darkness of iniquity has arisen. And do you wish likewise to learn from the prophet who they are that have "the abundance of peace"? Hear how he says in the psalms: "much peace to those who love your name, and there is no stumbling-block for them". "Days" therefore "of righteousness and abundance of peace shall arise" for "those who love the name of the Lord". But the impious too have their own light, from which doubtless "evil days" arise for them. And do you wish this too to be proved to you from the scriptures? Hear what is written: "light", it says, "is for the righteous always, but the light of the impious shall be extinguished". You see, then, that there is a certain "light proper to the impious", which "shall be extinguished", and a "light of the righteous", which remains "forever". And I do not know whether anyone would understand it so ineptly as to think that there is some other substantial light which is called "of the impious", and another which is "of the righteous". This assuredly can in no way be. For the light of the world made by God is one, which shines upon all in common and equally. But in the manner which we expounded above it must be understood that our soul is either "enlightened by the true light", which will never "be extinguished", which is Christ, or, if it does not have in itself that light which is eternal, it is doubtless enlightened by a temporal and extinguishable light from him "who transfigures himself into an angel of light" and enlightens the heart of the sinner with a false light, so that those things which are present and perishing seem to him to be good and splendid. By this light are enlightened those who call pleasure the highest good; by this light are enlightened those who seek riches and worldly honors and earthly glory as though the memorial of eternity. These too, then, are "in the days" of his light which "shall be extinguished" (for all these things which they do, which they desire and covet, shall be extinguished); by this light are enlightened also the heretics, who proclaim "knowledge falsely so called": hence Marcion, being enlightened, says that the God of the law is just, but not good. If therefore we have rightly understood who are the days that are enlightened by our Lord Jesus Christ, "the true light", and who are the days that are enlightened by him "who transfigures himself into an angel of light", and whose light "shall be extinguished", we can fittingly understand also those "days of Joshua" of which it is said that: "the people served the Lord all the days of Joshua"; for it is certain that whoever has in himself "the days of Jesus serves the Lord", nor can it come to pass that anyone having in himself "the days of Jesus" and "the light" of Christ should serve the devil or serve avarice; nor can it come to pass that one should be enlightened by the light of truth and serve falsehood, nor can one enlightened by the light of sanctification be a slave to lust and uncleanness. And so the Apostle too says: "for what participation is there of righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship of light with darkness? And what concord of Christ with Belial? Or what part has the faithful with the unfaithful?". Let us pray, therefore, that Christ, who is "the true light", may always make good days in us, and that never, with the devil enlightening us, may we have in us "evil days", of which the Apostle says: "redeeming the time, because the days are evil". For we have "evil days" when we seek carnal things instead of spiritual, earthly instead of heavenly, perishing things instead of eternal, present things instead of future. If ever, then, you see desires of this kind arising in you, know that you are set in "evil days" and most wicked ones; and therefore persist in prayers, that you may be freed from the "evil day" and, as the Apostle says, be delivered "from the present evil age"; for in the manner which we said above, not only do "days" become "evil", but the "age" too is made "evil".

"The people therefore served the Lord all the days of Joshua and all the days of the elders who were after Joshua". Blessed is he who "in the days of Jesus serves the Lord", who is enlightened by his word and his wisdom, who is illuminated by his precepts, who from his teaching receives the light of knowledge. Yet in the second place, and after this man, that man too is blessed who "serves the Lord in the days of the elders who were after Joshua". The "elders" who were either with Joshua or "after Joshua" — who are they but the Apostles, who also by their own writings and precepts enlighten our hearts and make in us likewise certain days out of that light which they themselves, coming, partook of from "the true light"? Whoever therefore is enlightened and instructed by the precepts of the Apostles and is trained by apostolic rules for the service of the Lord — this is the one who is said to "serve the Lord in the days of the elders who were after Joshua". And do you wish to see that, just as the Savior "was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world", so the Apostles too were "the light of the world"? In the Gospel it is written, the Lord saying to them: "you are the light of the world". But if the Apostles too are "the light of the world", doubtless by their precepts and commandments they enlighten for us "days" in which "we may serve the Lord".

But as for what he said: "all the days of the elders who were of longer days after Joshua", this too does not seem to me to be said idly, that the "elders who were after Joshua" are said to be "long-lived" or "of longer days". And indeed it belongs to God alone to know who, "after Joshua", among "the elders" made "a longer day", that is, who sent forth from himself a greater light — whether Paul or Peter, Bartholomew or John; yet the saints are said to be "of longer days". But on the contrary, then, when the world shall be filled with stumbling-blocks, when "with iniquity increasing the love of many shall grow cold", and when "the Son of man coming will scarcely find faith upon the earth", then the days to come are said not to be "long", but rather are said to be shortened, as the Lord said that: "unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved". Evil days, therefore, are said to be "shortened", but the good days in which "we serve the Lord" are "long-lived" and of much time and, as it were, of a great span. See, however, that he indicated this too in the Gospel, that: "for the sake of the elect those days shall be shortened". For "the elect", then, "the evil days shall be shortened", the days of iniquity and of stumbling; and, as I judge, once the "evil days" have begun to be "shortened" for the elect, they are always shortened and diminished, until they are reduced to nothing and utterly waste away and at last perish. Of these, I think, was that one too who said: "let that day perish, in which I was born!". Thus, therefore, "for the elect the evil days are shortened" and perish, but the days of the holy elders are long-lived and prolonged. But that too which occurs to us as we speak — and would that it may occur at the Lord's prompting — must not be passed over, namely that he said: "the people served the Lord all the days of Joshua"; he did not say that there was one day of Joshua, but "the days of Joshua" are many. What, then, are these many days that we posit according to this order which we have expounded? I judge thus, that one day of his is righteousness, another sanctification, another prudence, another mercy, and thus through the several good things of the virtues are the "days of Jesus" reckoned, in which "the Lord" is served, because in these virtues of the soul the Lord is pleased. But reckon also his patience a day, and his gentleness and piety and goodness, and call a day of his everything that pertains to virtue. And thus "in all the days of Jesus you will serve the Lord", that is, in all these virtues; for the instruction of holy Scripture does not will that you should have some of these virtues in yourself and neglect others, but that, adorned with all these virtues and set in the acts of them, you should "serve the Lord". And in the same way one has also in himself the "days of the elders" and "in their days serves the Lord", fulfilling that which the Apostle Paul says: "be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ".

"In the days", he says, "of their elders, who knew all the works of the Lord". Who is it that "knows all the works of the Lord", but he who does them? For just as it was said of the sons of Eli that they were "sons of pestilence, not knowing the Lord" — not that they were ignorant of the Lord, who were indeed even teachers of the rest, but because they acted as those act who do not know the Lord — in this way too it must here be understood, when he says: "who knew every work of the Lord". And not only, he says, "did they know the work of the Lord", but he added: "who knew every work of the Lord", that is, who "knew" both the work of the righteousness of the Lord and the work of sanctification and of patience and of gentleness and of piety; and everything whatsoever that comes from the commandments of God is called "the work of the Lord". But just as there is a work of the Lord, so there is doubtless a work of the devil contrary to it. For it is certain that, just as righteousness is the work of God, so also injustice is the work of the devil, and, just as gentleness is the work of God, so also anger or fury is the work of the devil. Those, therefore, are said to "have known" the work of God who do his work. But that it may become still clearer from the authority of the scriptures how Scripture is accustomed to speak of knowing or not knowing, see how it is also written elsewhere: "he who keeps", it says, the commandment "shall not know an evil word". Can it come to pass that "he who keeps the commandment" should "not know evil words"? He does indeed know them, but he is said "not to know" for this reason, that he guards against them and avoids them. But also, as regards what was said of the Lord and Savior himself, that he "knew no sin", it is certain that he is said to have "been ignorant of sin" for this reason, that he did not do the work of sin. In this way, then, he too is said to "know the works of the Lord" who does "the works of the Lord". But he is ignorant of the work of God who does not do the work of God.

But how do we pass over this too, which he added: "who knew the great works of the Lord, which he did in Israel"? For what? Are there any "works of the Lord" that are small, in distinction from which these are called "great"? I judge that every work of God is indeed great, but according to the capacity of those for whom he works, if they be compared with one another, the works of the Lord are said to be either great or small. For example, he led the sons of Israel out of Egypt "with a strong hand" and "an exalted arm"; when Egypt had been smitten with heavenly prodigies, he "made a way in the sea"; he gave manna in the desert to the people; he spoke "from heaven" to Moses; he gave the law written "on tablets of stone". Are not these "great works of God"? But if you compare with these the fact that "God so loved this world that he gave his only Son" for the salvation of the world, you will find that all those are small in comparison with the greatness of this work. Which work we too must both know and believe, and must work "the works of the Lord", not negligently, but faithfully and attentively, so that we too may be found "in the days of Jesus" Christ and "in the days of the elders", his holy Apostles, with whom may we deserve also to receive the fellowship of the heavenly inheritance, through our Lord Jesus Christ himself, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The death of Jesus too has been read to us. That he, indeed, "the son of Nun", "died" is no wonder; for he paid what was owed to nature. But since we had undertaken to refer these things, which were read concerning the son of Nun, to our Lord Jesus Christ, we must see how it may fittingly be said even of him that: "Jesus died". I think — speaking this too, however, according to the authority of Scripture — that in some Jesus lives, but in some he has "died". In Paul Jesus lives, and in Peter, and in all those who can deservedly say: "and now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me". And again he says: "for me to live is Christ, and to die is gain". In such men as these, therefore, Jesus is deservedly said to "live". But in whom has "Jesus died"? In those, without doubt, who by repenting often and again transgressing are said as it were to insult the death of Jesus; concerning whom the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, says: "crucifying again to themselves the Son of God and holding him up to mockery". You see, then, that in those who sin "Jesus" is said not only to "die", but is even asserted to be "crucified" by them and "mocked". But do you yourself also consider within yourself, whether, when you think of avarice and desire to plunder what belongs to others, you can then say that "Christ lives in me". Or if you think of debauchery, if you are driven by rage, if you are inflamed with spite, if you are goaded by envy, if you rave in drunkenness, if you are lifted up with pride, if you rush on in cruelty — can you in all these say that: "Christ lives in me"? Thus, therefore, "Christ dies" in those who sin, in that righteousness works nothing in them, patience nothing, truth nothing, nor all those things which Christ is. But whatever the saints do, it is Christ who is said to work these things, just as the Apostle also says: "I can do all things in him who strengthens me, Christ". And the Lord himself too gave a most beautiful distinction concerning this in the Gospels, when he says: "whoever confesses in me before men, I also will confess in him before my Father, who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before men, I also will deny him before my Father". You have seen that of those who "confess in himself" he said "he confesses", as one who himself lives in them and works the works of life. But in those "who deny" he did not keep the same likeness of the word, so as to say that whoever denies in me, I too will deny in him, but "whoever denies me before men, I too will deny him before my Father", to show that he who indeed "denies" is outside of himself, whereas he who "confesses" is in himself. Therefore for this reason here too Scripture says that, when "Jesus had died", "there arose another generation after those, who did not know Jesus and the works which he did in Israel".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And the children of Israel did what was wicked before God". Almighty God, our ruler, grant that it may never happen to us that Jesus Christ, after he has risen from the dead, should again die in us. For what does it profit me if in others he lives by virtue and in me he dies by the weakness of sin? What does it profit me if in me and in my heart he does not live, and if in me he does not accomplish the works of life? What does it profit me if in another he is nourished and refreshed by good pursuits, by good faith, by good works, but in me and in my heart he is in a manner suffocated and slain by evil thoughts and unspeakable desires, by the worst pursuits? For see what Scripture adds, that: "there arose", it says, "another generation, which did not know Jesus and the great works which he did". That "generation, which did not know" the Lord "Jesus", is the one of "evil thoughts" and the worst desires, which "proceeds from the heart". This is the "generation which does not know" the Lord "Jesus", nor "the great work which he did in Israel". You see that sinners come to such a point that they even forget that "great" and glorious "work which the Lord did", that he was crucified "for our sins, and rose again for our justification". Whence I believe that, fearing this forgetfulness, the Apostle said to his disciple Timothy, whom he held as especially dear: "be mindful that Christ Jesus has risen from the dead". For he knew that of this so great a work, that "he rose from the dead", forgetfulness could come to be, if a sinful generation should arise in the heart. "There did" therefore "what was wicked before the Lord" "another generation, which knew not Jesus" nor the elders.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And it served", it says, "the Baalim, and they forsook the Lord God of their fathers". These things indeed the ancients did, but since the things that are written are said to have been written not for their sake, but "for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come", let us see whether these things may seem to be said in greater part of us than of them. And do you wish to see that not by me, but by the Apostle these things are expounded as being about us? Hear himself what he says: "but in Elijah what does the Scripture say, how he pleads with God against Israel? Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have torn down your altars, and I am left alone, and they seek my life. But what does the divine answer say to him? I have left for myself seven thousand men, who have not bent the knee to Baal" — and he adds: "so therefore", he says, "also at this present time a remnant according to the election of grace has been made safe". You see, then, that those who "bent the knee to the Baalim" and "those who did not bend it" he interprets of the remnant of believers and of the multitude of unbelievers. And this he shows: that those who in the time of the Savior proved unbelieving and impious "bent the knee to the Baalim" and adored idols, but those who believe and fulfill the works of faith "did not bend the knee to the Baalim". For nowhere is it reported in the histories or in the Gospels or in any other writings whatever that anyone in the time of the Savior bent the knee to idols, but assuredly this is said of those who, bound and as it were fettered by their sins, were held fast. Whence it is evident that we too, as often as we sin and "are led captive in the law of sin", "bend our knees to the Baalim". But we were not called to this, nor did we believe for this, that we should again serve sin and again "bend the knee" to the devil, but that we should "bend the knee in the name of Jesus", because "in the name of Jesus every knee is bent, of things in heaven and things on earth and things beneath the earth", and that we should bend "our knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named". But what does it profit me if I "bend the knees" of my body to God, coming to prayer, and "bend the knees" of my heart to the devil? For if I do not "stand firm against the wiles of the devil", I have "bent my knees" to the devil. And if I do not "stand" steadfastly "against" anger, I have "bent my knees" to anger. Likewise, if I do not steadfastly resist lust, I have "bent" the "knees" of my heart to lust. And in each single thing that is contrary to God I shall be seen to do this, unless I "stand" steadfastly and bravely, just as those also did who "worshipped the Baalim and forsook the God of their fathers", who "brought them out of the land of Egypt". Let us not therefore suppose that, because we seem not to worship idols, these things for that reason do not pertain also to some of us. Whatever each one worships above the rest, whatever he admires and loves above all things, this is his God. Indeed, this is what before all things and above all things God demands of man by his commandment: "you shall love", he says, "the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength" — desiring in a manner to lay first claim to himself upon all the affections of the human mind, and knowing that whatever one "loves with all the heart and with all the soul and with all the strength", this is his God. Let each one now examine himself and silently reckon up from his own heart what flame of love above all else and beyond all things burns hottest in him, what affection is cherished in him more ardent than the rest. Do you yourselves hold judgment concerning these things, weigh them on the balance of your own examination, and if there be anything that outweighs in the scale of love, this is your God. But I fear that in very many the love of gold outweighs, and that the weight of avarice, pressing the scale down enough, sinks it. And to such a one it will surely be said: "you cannot serve God and mammon" — that is, avarice. I fear too in others that the love of lust and pleasure outweighs so far as to sink it to the ground; in others that the love of worldly glory and the desire for human dignity weighs down above all; and I think there are very few who, measuring within themselves their own affections and weighing them in the equal balance of the scale, find that the weight of the love of God outweighs above all other things that are human. I know one who had weighed these things within himself with the utmost scrutiny, and, when he had found that all the affections which were within him inclined to that side where the love of God was, said with all confidence that: "neither death nor life nor angels nor powers, neither things present nor things to come nor height nor depth nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord". But this is Paul, who could so speak these things, because "neither things present nor things to come nor any other creature can separate him from the love of God". But as for us — would that we might say even this, that neither gold nor silver nor the pleasure of the flesh nor the glory of the world and fleeting, temporal dignity, nor bodily delights, nor the favor of children or of a spouse "will be able to separate us from the love of God". Surely let it at least be permitted to us to say with confidence that neither the love of secular literature nor the sophistries of the philosophers nor the deceptions of the astrologers and the feigned courses of the stars, nor the divinations contrived by the stealthy deceit of demons, nor any love of foreknowledge whatsoever, sought through those things which are not lawful, "will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus". Or did not the whole error of the heathen take its beginning from this, when they will that those things which men greatly love should be gods, and ascribe the divine name to any human vices and desires? For those greedy for money and burning with the love of avarice call Mammon, as among the Syrians, the god of that greed; the lovers of lust and pleasure ascribe to themselves Venus as the goddess of this vice by which they are driven. Likewise in the other vices too they have made this very affection, by which they are urged on, their God. Whence the Apostle also says the same thing; for he says: "and avarice, which is the worship of idols". You see, then, that not only to adore an idol, but even to be devoted to "avarice" is reckoned "the worship of idols" and slavery. So therefore we too, when we are so given over to certain vices that we "love them with all our heart and with all our soul and with all our strength", are said to adore idols and "to have gone after strange gods".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And they adored", it says, "strange gods, the gods of the nations who were round about them, and they provoked the Lord to anger". See how much sins accomplish, that we who sin are said to provoke to anger him in whom there is not only no affection of anger, but not even any other passible movement. Truly he remains unchangeable in his nature and is never disturbed by the affections of anger; but I, through the things in which I transgress, decree anger for myself, just as the Apostle says, teaching this very thing: "but according to your hardness and impenitent heart you treasure up", he says, "for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will render to each one according to his works".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Therefore "they provoked the Lord to anger, and forsook the Lord, they worshipped Baal and Astarte. And the Lord was angry with fury against Israel, and delivered them into the hands of plunderers". As long as one serves God, he is not "delivered into the hands of plunderers". But when he has "forsaken the Lord" and has begun to serve his own passions, then it is said of him that: "God delivered them into passions of ignominy", and again: "he delivered them into a reprobate mind, that they should do those things which are not fitting". Why? Because "they are filled", he says, "with all iniquity, wickedness, fornication, avarice", and all the rest that are named — just as here too now, since "they served", it says, "and adored the Baalim and Astarte, God delivered them into the hands of plunderers; and it came to pass in the hands of their enemies". For these things, as I have already often said, the Jews read as histories of deeds done and past. But "we", "for whose sake these things" are said to be "written", ought to know that, if we have sinned against the Lord and worship the pleasures of our soul and the desires of the flesh as it were as God, we too are delivered up, and by apostolic authority are handed over into the hands of the devil. Hear, then, himself saying of him who had sinned: "I have delivered", he says, "such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved". You see, then, that even now not only through his Apostles does God "deliver" transgressors "into the hands of enemies", but also through those who preside over the church and have the power not only of loosing, but also of binding, sinners "are delivered into the destruction of the flesh", when for their offenses they are separated from the body of Christ. And, as it seems to me, even now men are delivered from the church into the power of the devil in two ways: in this manner which we spoke of above, when his offense becomes manifest to the church and he is driven from the church by the priests, so that, marked out by men, he may blush, and being converted there may befall him that which follows: "that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ"; but in another way one is "delivered to the devil" when his sin does not become manifest to men, yet God, "who sees in secret", perceiving his mind and his soul serving vices and passions, and that in his heart it is not he who is worshipped, but either avarice or lust or vainglory or other such things — such a one the Lord himself "delivers to Satan". How does he "deliver him to Satan"? He departs from his mind and turns himself away and flees from his evil thoughts and unworthy desires and leaves the "house" of his heart "empty". And then there shall be fulfilled in that man what is written: "but when the unclean spirit has gone out from a man, he goes about through dry places: and if he does not find rest, he returns to his own house; and finding it vacant and swept, he takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and entering he dwells in that house; and then the last state of that man becomes worse than the first". In this manner, then, it must be understood that God "delivers up" those whom he delivers, not that he himself delivers anyone, but from the fact that he forsakes the unworthy — those, namely, who do not so cultivate themselves and purge themselves from vices that God should gladly dwell in them. When he himself flees and turns away from a soul which is set in uncleanness and vices, it is said to be delivered up from the fact that it is found empty of God and is invaded by the wicked spirit. And therefore let us with the utmost zeal be watchful and hasten to purge ourselves from vices and evil desires, that we may be able to hold God within us and that he may deign to dwell in us, while he is delighted both with our acts and our words and our thoughts, if we conduct according to his will all things that we do, so that, "whether we eat, or whether we drink, or whether we do anything else, we may do all in the name of" our "Lord" Jesus Christ, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When "the children of Israel did evil in the sight of God, and forgot the Lord their God," and, forsaking him, "served the Baalim and the groves" of the nations, then, "storing up wrath for themselves," they "were handed over," by the just judgment of God, "into the hands of their enemies," according to what the present reading has declared: "into the hands," it says, "of Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia." Now Cushan-rishathaim is interpreted as "their humiliation". They "were handed over," therefore, "into the hands" of him who would humiliate them. And because they themselves were acting impiously against the Most High upon the high places of the mountains, for that reason they are handed over by him into humiliation. But I would not have you think that this divine providence was directed only toward the ancients — namely, that it handed over those who impiously exalted themselves to be humbled, and by a saving method of medicine cured contraries with contraries — while now the omnipotent God lacks toward his Church such a saving providence. There is even now a "Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia," to whom are handed over to be humbled and afflicted the souls that, despising Christian humility, have given themselves over to pride and arrogance. The vice of pride is exceedingly hateful in the sight of God, since, as Scripture says: "the beginning of departing from God is pride," and again elsewhere Scripture says: "God resists the proud, but to the humble he gives grace." If, therefore, anyone, despising the humility of Christ — who for our sake, "though he was God, was made man and humbled himself even unto death" — is lifted up and exalted, leaps forward toward the powers and dignities of the world, and does not shrink or shudder at the arts by which he strives to attain these things, even though they be against faith and religion, provided only he obtain what he desires, it comes about thereby that he "does evil in the sight of the Lord"; and after he has gained the highest insignia of the powers and has climbed to the very topmost heights of pride, cast down from there he "is handed over" to this "Cushan-rishathaim," that is, to one of the "airy princes" — as elsewhere Pharaoh, and elsewhere Hiram — that he may humble the one who had been too greatly exalted, that he may afflict and crush him, until he comes to his senses and seeks the Lord; because, while he was set in pride and elation, he did not know God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now therefore let us see what these do who are handed over on account of sin and set in tribulation. Precisely that which is written: "and they cried out to the Lord when they were in tribulation, and he delivered them out of their distresses." "And he led them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and burst their bonds asunder." But each one of us also — even if he be small, even if he be the least, even if he enjoy no dignity in the world — can be afflicted with the vice of pride; and nothing is so foul nor so execrable, as Scripture says, as "a poor man who is proud and a rich man who is a liar." Sometimes, however, this disease of pride penetrates not only the poor of the common people, but strikes even the priestly and Levitical order itself. You may find sometimes even among us certain persons — we who are set as an example of humility and placed in the circle of the altar like mirrors, as it were, for those who look on — in whom the vice of arrogance reeks, and from the altar of the Lord, which ought to be fragrant with the sweetness of incense, there gleams forth the most foul odor of pride and elation. But let this most foul odor, I beg, be cast out from all this holy Church and especially from those who minister in holy things, so that we may be able, as Paul said, to be made "the good odor of Christ"; "lest perhaps the Lord be angered" and "we provoke the Holy One of Israel to wrath" and he "hand" us "over into the hands of Cushan-rishathaim," so that the humility which we ought to have taught in the knowledge of Christ we may learn in the tribulation of our chastisement. But behold the kindly Lord mingling mercy with severity and weighing the very measure of the punishment with a just and clement balance. He did not hand over the offenders forever, but for as long a time, he says, as they served the Baalim, for that same length they also "serve Cushan-rishathaim," that is, "for eight years." Learn this, you too, O hearer, whoever you are who are conscious to yourself of some error. And for however long a time you know yourself to have gone astray, for however long a time you have transgressed, for that same length of time nonetheless humble yourself before God and make satisfaction to him in the confession of repentance. Do not wait for Cushan-rishathaim to humble you and for necessity to wring repentance from you against your will, but do you yourself forestall the hands of that torturer, because, if you amend yourself, if you correct yourself, God is holy and merciful, and he tempers his vengeance from the one who forestalls it by repenting. But let us also consider this, that, so long as these who had been handed over for their offenses "served Cushan-rishathaim" and did not "cry out to the Lord," no one was raised up who could save them. But when "they cried out to the Lord, then the Lord raised up a Savior for Israel and saved them."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now he calls Othniel the Savior, who is interpreted as "the time of God for me". Through this Othniel, therefore, that former people was snatched from the servitude of humiliation, and peace was restored to the people — the peace which pride and the various crimes of the people had for a while put to flight. But since we have said that a certain Cushan-rishathaim can be understood spiritually, both as a king and as one of the adversaries and a prince among the "airy powers," so it seems to me consequent that this Othniel too, who was raised up to deliver the people, is some one of the "heavenly host" and of the archangelic troops which "are sent as a help to those who obtain the inheritance of salvation"; and there are saving angels who are designated under the figure either of Othniel or of Ehud, because, as we have often shown, we are not only assailed by the contrary powers, but the divine and good powers too are sent by the Lord for our help. Let us see, nevertheless, who this Othniel was, of what family, of what nobility. "The son," it says, of Kenaz, "the brother of Caleb" — that praiseworthy and admirable man Caleb, who was the companion and comrade of Joshua son of Nun, concerning whom, as far as we were able, we have discoursed in their proper places, as seemed good.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: What, then, does Scripture say concerning this Othniel? After it had said that "the children of Israel cried out to the Lord," "the Spirit of the Lord came," it says, "upon Othniel, and he judged Israel." Do you suppose there is among us anyone who so "sends forth to the Lord a cry" so strong and so just that he is worthy to be heard, and the people deserve to receive a judge — and such a judge, one whom the "Spirit of God" may fill, that he may be able to hold to right judgment? Whence also the book itself is called the book of Judges, and in it are described the judges who judged the people. For just as other books are called the books of Kings, or of Kingdoms, in which is described each of the kings, how he reigned and what he did, so also in this little book the deeds of the Judges are recounted, and there is described not only whatever was done rightly and usefully by them, but also whatever was blamably committed. Yet if you ask why both are described, it is this: that now the leaders or judges of the Church, perceiving those things which were done praiseworthily by them, may follow the examples of the former ones; but if any things in them are blamed, that these may beware and turn aside. Great praise, therefore, of this first judge Othniel is recounted, in that "the Spirit of God came upon him" and through the Spirit of God he "judged Israel," which I do not well remember to have been said of any other. There are therefore even today very many judges of all the churches which are under heaven, to whom has been given the judgment not only of deeds done, but also of souls. But I do not know whether there is any such judge of the Church whom "God makes worthy to fill with his Spirit," so that, just as this Othniel was adorned with the testimony of Scripture, so also they themselves, for whom we wish this, may deserve the testimony of God. He says therefore: "and the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he judged Israel. And he went out to war, and the Lord handed over into his hands Cushan-rishathaim the king." Why this? Because the "Spirit of the Lord" was in him, and "his hand was strengthened over Cushan-rishathaim."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And after this it says: "the land had rest under him as judge for forty years." You see how bountiful is the divine clemency. "For eight years the children of Israel had served" for the offenses of many; "for forty years" they endure in peace for the righteousness of one.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But what is said after this? "And Othniel," it says, "the son of Kenaz, died." I see a perilous matter. "Othniel died." Why? Because the people was now unworthy to have such a judge. Then in what follows, after he had died, it says: "and the children of Israel added," it says, "to do evil in the sight of the Lord; and the Lord strengthened Eglon king of Moab against Israel." Consider that, because they were now unworthy to have such a leader, for that reason the good judge is taken away from them. And because they "did evil in the sight of the Lord," there is stirred up against them a most wicked enemy, "Eglon king of Moab." You see that our sins supply strength to our enemies, and that, when we "do evil in the sight of the Lord" and transgress, then our adversaries "are strengthened by the Lord," then strength is given to the contrary powers. Whether you seek this according to the letter, you will find it so, that the enemies would not grow strong unless our offenses conferred strength upon them; or whether you consider it in spiritual things, likewise the contrary powers would not grow strong against us, nor would the devil himself prevail at all in us, unless we supplied him strength out of our vices; he would be very weak against us, unless we made him strong in sinning, and unless through our sins he found a place of entering and of dominating within us. For this reason, finally, the Apostle too gives warning beforehand, saying: "do not give place to the devil," just as here too we have just now read that, after "the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord," they "gave place to the devil." For "the Lord strengthened Eglon king of Moab, and joined to him all the sons of Ammon and Amalek." Not only, it says, was he himself "strengthened" out of the sins of the children of Israel, but there are joined to him wicked allies "from the sons of Ammon and Amalek," who together with him assail Israel.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And the children of Israel served," it says, "Eglon king of Moab for eighteen years." Observe that divine Scripture indicates even the measures of the punishment; there it says "for eight years" and here "for eighteen." Now it is certain that according to the measure of the sin and the delay of our conversion the times of chastisement too are determined.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: For these "eighteen years" of servitude also passed, and it is not recounted that "they cried out to the Lord" or were converted from their wickedness, but after eighteen years it is again said that: "the children of Israel cried out to the Lord, and the Lord raised up for them a Savior, Ehud the son of Gera, the son of Gemini, a man ambidextrous." Behold what manner of man this is who is raised up to save Israel! He has nothing left-handed in himself, but has both hands as a right hand; for this is what is meant by "ambidextrous." Truly a worthy leader of the people and judge of the Church, who does nothing left-handed, whose "right hand knows not what his left hand does," who is right-handed on either side — right-handed in faith, right-handed in deeds — who has nothing of those who are placed "on the left," to whom it is said: "depart from me, you workers of iniquity, I know you not; go into the eternal fire which God has prepared for the devil and his angels." And if in such matters it is permitted to presume from what is similar, I think that according to the spiritual understanding all the saints too are called "ambidextrous," and on the contrary the devil and his princes, if it may be said, are called ambi-sinistrous. For all that they do is left-handed, all perverse, all consigned to the eternal fire together with those who are "on the left."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: To the rule of Ehud the ambidextrous is joined the rule of Shamgar. But let us see how Ehud, who is interpreted "praise," brought his rule to a close. The narrative has taught us those things which are written concerning Eglon the king, how this most wise Ehud, using a certain artifice and, so to speak, a cunning but praiseworthy deception, slew Eglon the tyrant, who is interpreted "whirling" or "of the wheel-track." Such, then, ought the judges of our people also to be, as was that Ehud who is interpreted "praise," so that they may cut down all the whirling motions and wheel-tracks of the evil path and destroy the king of the Midianites. Now the Midianites are interpreted "flowing" or "outpouring." Who, then, can be seen or understood to be the prince or leader of this fluid and dissolute nation, other than the discourse of that philosophy which judges pleasure to be the highest good — whom the Gospel discourse, which is compared to a sword, may slay and destroy? And let the prophetic word itself be shut up in their belly and in the innermost vitals by the disputations of the "ambidextrous" teacher, so that, confining them by the assertion of truth, he may extinguish every "thought" of a depraved doctrine and gross understanding "that exalts and raises itself up against the spiritual knowledge of Christ"; so that, doing thus and contending in the word of God, each judge of the Church may himself also become that praiseworthy Ehud, of whom the Lord may say: "Well done, good and faithful servant, thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will set thee over many things".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us see what this "ambidextrous" judge does. "The children of Israel sent," it says, "gifts to Eglon king of the Moabites by the hand of Ehud"; "and Ehud made himself a sword sharpened on both sides, of the length of an extended palm, and girded it to himself upon his right thigh." You see that everything is right-handed which this "ambidextrous" "Ehud" carries out: he is right-handed both in hands and right-handed in feet. For he carries the sword on his right thigh, that he may come to the "king of Moab" and slay him. We had said above that these whom God is said to raise up for the salvation of the people and for the delivering of the children of Israel — the saviors or judges — bear the image of certain princes from the "heavenly host" and of the supernal powers, which God sends forth for the aid of those who cry out to him with their whole heart and by the conversion of repentance have bent the divine clemency toward themselves. But lest this seem to have been presumed by us in the eyes of our hearers, we ought to establish it from the authority of the Scriptures. It is written in Exodus that our fathers the children of Israel, when for a long time they had served the Egyptians and Pharaoh, that most harsh king, in the making of "mud and brick," "cried out," it says, "to the Lord," so that the Lord himself said: "the cry of the children of Israel has ascended to me," and, having sent Moses, he led them out visibly. But Scripture recounts that an exterminating angel was sent, who indeed laid waste all the firstborn of Egypt, but touched none of the Israelites. And thus it is declared that it was a heavenly power which, after the Egyptians had been laid waste and cast down, led the children of Israel out from the yoke of servitude. Something similar is also recounted in the histories, that under Sennacherib king of the Assyrians "an angel of the Lord" is sent, who, having slain and cast down in a single night "one hundred and eighty-five thousand" of the enemy, delivered both the city from the siege and the people from imminent destruction. So therefore even now we ought to observe the same consequence, that, if ever for our sins we are handed over into captivity, we should "cry out to the Lord." But let us cry out not with the mouth, but with the mind, so that the grief of the heart may "bring forth a fountain of tears from the eyes," like him who said: "every night will I wash my bed, I will water my couch with my tears." If we are so converted from evils that we no longer touch evils, if we so cease from pride that we no longer relish anything proud, anything arrogant, the Lord will send us too his heavenly power, through which we may be delivered from the yoke of diabolical servitude; a power which may do all things for us right-handed and prosperous, which may make us forsake the "left-hand way, which leads to perdition," and call us back to the true "way," him who says: "I am the way and the truth and the life," Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But having briefly gone back over these matters from the earlier reading — that is, over the end of Ehud — let us now see what sort the beginning of Shamgar is also, who is there interpreted "stranger." For it is true that all who are men of God are strangers in this world and sojourners upon the earth, just as was also he who said that: "I am a sojourner with thee upon the earth and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were". And so the Holy Spirit there calls this Shamgar too a sojourner — that is, here. For what is "there" to the Holy Spirit, who is in the heavens, is "here" to us. What, then, is said of Shamgar? "He smote", it says, "the Philistines, six hundred men, with the handle — or "foot" — of a plow". I see another kind of praise in Shamgar: this one fights with a "plow". Ehud was fighting with a sword, this one with a plow. Yet this one too conquers, overcomes, and lays low the Philistines. It can happen, therefore, that a judge of the Church does not always bring forth the sword — that is, does not always use the austerity of the word and the sharpness of correction — but sometimes also imitates the farmer, and, as it were plowing the soil of the soul and often cutting it open with a gentle admonition, prepares it, fit for receiving the seeds. Thus the Philistines will be slain in this way too, when we use not arguments and sharpness against our adversaries, but drive out vices and sins from the souls of our hearers by a rustic and simple admonition. But you also yourself, O hearer, be the farmer of your own soul; use this plow which Shamgar uses. But when "you have put your hand to the plow", do not "look back" — that is, after "you have taken up your cross and followed Christ", after you have renounced the world and the things which are in the world, do not "look back", do not seek again those things which "for the sake of Christ you had counted as dung", because, if you always keep your "hand upon this plow", so that you may confidently say: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world", then, as you say these things, "there shall fall at your right hand ten thousand, and at your left hand a thousand, but unto you they shall not come near". But this very thing also that it said, that "Shamgar smote the Philistines, six hundred of them", does not seem to me to have been said idly. For what need was there to designate even the number? Unless perhaps in the number itself it indicated more plainly those things of which we spoke above. For the number six, which multiplied comes to six hundred, holds the figure of this world, which is said to have been completed in six days. "Six hundred", therefore, he is said "to have smitten with the plow", he to whom "through the cross of Christ the world is crucified".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But what is added after this? "And the children of Israel", it says, "added to do evil in the sight of the Lord; and Ehud was dead". Undoubtedly in these matters too there is preserved that observation which we pointed out in the preceding passages: that for the sins of the people the good leader of the people dies. For when they have been made unworthy and have "done evil in the sight of God", the man of God will be taken away from them. But perhaps our people will say: when is the Church of God without a judge? Even if the former departs, another is supplied. Perhaps we shall say something bold, yet we say what is written. Not always is the prince of the people and judge of the Church given by the judgment of God, but according as our merits demand. If our deeds are evil and we "work evil in the sight of God", princes are given to us according to our heart; and this I will prove to you from the Scriptures. For hear what the Lord says: "They made themselves a king and not by me, and a prince and not by my counsel". And this seems to be said of that Saul, whom indeed the Lord himself had chosen and had commanded to be made king; but because he had been chosen not according to the will of God, but according to the merit of a sinful people, he denies that he was appointed with his will or counsel. Let us understand, then, that some such thing happens in the churches also, that according to the merits of the people either a ruler of the Church powerful in word and deed is granted by God or, if "the people do evil in the sight of the Lord", such a judge of the Church is given under whom the people may suffer "hunger and thirst", "not a hunger of bread nor a thirst of water, but a hunger of hearing the word of God". So, then, let us act, and so let us pray, that the divine displeasure may never condemn us in a "hunger of the word" and a "thirst", that there may never be taken away from us one who may instruct us in word and deed, who may furnish to the peoples out of himself a perfect example in conduct and integrity, in patience and meekness. For if we "do evil in the sight of the Lord" — that is, if we act wickedly, if we do our own will and not God's — then "Ehud dies" for us also, Shamgar is taken away, and our praise will be darkened, and we will be "delivered into the hands of Jabin king of Canaan". Now "Jabin" is interpreted "sense" or "prudence." If, therefore, we "do not approve to have God in our knowledge, God delivers us up unto a reprobate sense, filled", it says, "with iniquity, wickedness, fornication, covetousness, full of envy, murders, contention, deceit, whisperers, backbiters, hateful to God, injurious, proud, haughty, disobedient to parents, disorderly, without affection, without mercy". You see who and of what sort are they who "are delivered up unto a reprobate sense", who "are delivered up to Jabin the prince of the Canaanites".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And the prince", it says, "of the army of Jabin was Sisera, and he himself dwelt in Harosheth of the Gentiles, and he had nine hundred iron chariots. And the children of Israel cried out to the Lord". In this too there is likewise kept that observation which we designated above: that the children of Israel do not know how "to cry out to the Lord", except when "they have been delivered into the hands of Jabin", or when they are afflicted through his "prince of the army, Sisera", who "had", it says, "nine hundred iron chariots", by which of course the people of stiff neck was afflicted. Now "Sisera" is interpreted "vision of a horse." For he is the "animal" and not the "spiritual" man, who sees nothing except those things which are "animal"; that is his vision, that is ever his gaze.
