And therefore the "animal man" and "he who is according to the flesh" always "persecutes him who is according to the spirit", until the "spiritual" man understands and "examines all things" and understands whence help is to be sought for himself, and "cries out to the Lord", until, for that soul which "has cried out to the Lord", there is raised up prophecy, which is in the figure of Deborah, and according to the grace and understanding of prophecy either the people of the Church may be governed or even the sense of each mind and soul may be ruled, through Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us see, then, whether perhaps through these things we may be taught something worthy, as also from the other Scriptures, concerning the more hidden mysteries. First, this very fact that, although many men are reported to have been judges in Israel, of none of them is it said that he was a "prophet" except of "Deborah the woman." Even the very first surface of the letter itself furnishes no small consolation to the female sex in this, and it summons them, that they should by no means despair, on account of the weakness of their sex, of being able to become capable even of the grace of prophecy, but that they should understand and believe that purity of mind, not diversity of sex, merits this grace. But let us see what secret of the inner understanding also breathes forth here. "Deborah" is interpreted as "bee or speech". But we have already said in the earlier passages too that Deborah is to be taken as a figure of prophecy, which is the bee. For it is certain that all prophecy composes the sweet honeycombs of heavenly doctrine and the sweet honey of the divine utterance. Whence David also sang, saying: "how sweet are your utterances to my throat, above honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!" And again elsewhere he says "that the judgments of God are precious above gold and the precious stone exceedingly, and sweeter above honey and the honeycomb."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We pass from questions to questions and from mysteries to mysteries, and while we can scarcely and with difficulty explain each of the first things, more difficult matters follow upon the difficult ones — matters which do not so much require the eloquence of human talent as they demand the inspiration of divine grace. For without doubt the hearer will ask — since indeed there is that saying of the Apostle Paul which declares: "all Scripture divinely inspired is useful for teaching, for reproof, for instruction which is in righteousness" — what this Scripture has in itself (which we likewise without doubt confess to be divinely inspired) that may yield to us "for instruction," that may yield "for reproof," that may yield "for discipline," that may yield "for righteousness." For what is conferred upon us from this, if we read what has just been recited — that is, that "Deborah," it says, "a woman, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she herself judged Israel at that time; and she," it says, "Deborah, sat under a palm tree between the middle of Ramah and the middle of Bethel, on Mount Ephraim, and the sons of Israel went up to her, that they might be judged"? And then, what erudition or teaching or righteousness do those things confer upon us which follow, whether concerning Barak or concerning Jael or even concerning Sisera, "the commander of the army of Jabin"?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us also consider this — where the prophecy is said to "reside" and where its place is described. "Under a palm tree," it says, "between the middle of Ramah and the middle of Bethel." Prophecy has its seat "under a palm tree," because "the righteous man," says David, "will flourish like a palm tree" — through this, that prophecy leads the one instructed by its teachings to the "palm of the heavenly calling of God, in Christ Jesus our Lord." And it is said to sit "between the middle of Ramah and the middle of Bethel." "Ramah" is interpreted as "heights". "Bethel," however, as "the house of God". See in what places "prophecy" is said to "reside" — between the heights and the house of God. For nothing lowly, nothing cast down, nothing base can be found near the seat of prophecy; just as Solomon likewise, describing the seat of wisdom, says of it that she either "stands at the gates of the cities" or dwells "on the ramparts of the walls" or "acts freely" in the high towers. In this way, then, prophecy, which is now described in Deborah, is said to dwell between the house of God and the heights. For it does not teach us "to seek the things that are upon the earth, but the things that are in the heavens and in the heights, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God": thither prophecy exhorts us to ascend, thither it strives to set its disciples.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: This prophecy, therefore, first of all, it says, "sent and called Barak to herself." Now "Barak" is interpreted as "flashing". But a flashing is that which has light indeed, but not lasting; for it shines forth for a little while and ceases. This Barak, therefore, seems to me to bear the figure of the former people, who first of all was called through prophecy and invited to hear the utterances of God and to receive the gifts of the divine law — who indeed shone and flashed in the splendor of the law for a brief time, but did not long endure nor was able to obtain the continuous brightness of the light. When, therefore, Deborah had said to Barak — that is, prophecy to the former people — that: "the Lord God of Israel has commanded you, and do you go up onto Mount Tabor, and take ten thousand men" and the rest that is written, let us see what Barak, in the person of the people, answered to prophecy: "I will not go up," he says, "unless you also go up with me, because I do not know the day on which the Lord will send his angel with me." You see, then, how prophecy delivered to those former ones the utterances of God and says that the commands were given to them, that they should "go up onto the mountain"; but they excuse themselves and say: "I will not go up unless you too go up with me." And as regards the excuse it is indeed true, but as regards the promise it is false. For that they "did not go up" onto the mountain of God is certain; but that they promise they will go up together with prophecy is false. For they did not follow prophecy, so as to believe in him concerning whom all prophecy was written beforehand, Christ. Therefore, then, Deborah says to him: "I will go with you. Nevertheless know that the primacy will not be yours on this way which you tread, but into the hand of a woman the Lord will deliver Sisera." She clearly shows that "the primacy will not be" with that people, nor will the palm of victory abide with it, "but into the hand of a woman," whose name was Jael, "Sisera will be delivered."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now it is described that, when according to the admonition of Deborah — that is, of prophecy — Barak pursued Sisera the leader of the Philistines, he himself indeed could not seize him, but there met him "as he fled" a foreign woman, Jael, which woman had previously held a covenant of friendship with him; "to whom," when he had "turned aside" for the sake of hiding, he asked for water to drink, but by her "he was given milk to drink"; and when she had placed him "in hiding" and had covered him with skins, after this she drove a stake, driven in "with a mallet," through his cheeks — or "jaws" — and fixed it fast: and then, "meeting" Barak as he pursued, she "showed Sisera" "now dead" and laid low.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: What, then, does all this text of the history show us of the mystery? "Jael," that foreign "woman" concerning whom prophecy said that the victory would come to pass "into the hand of a woman," holds the figure of the Church, which has been gathered from the foreign nations. Now "Jael" is interpreted as "ascent", because in truth there is no other ascent by which one may ascend to heaven except "through the Church of the manifold wisdom of God." She, therefore, is the one who, while she ascends from bodily things to spiritual and from earthly to heavenly, slays Sisera — of whom we have already said above that he holds the figure of the carnal vices and of the "animal" or "earthy" man, because Sisera is interpreted as "the sight of a horse", concerning which Scripture says: "do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding." With a stake, therefore, she slays him — that is, she lays him low with the sharp point and power of the wood of the cross. And not without cause is she described as having pierced through his "jaws" with the stake. For that mouth which spoke of carnal things, and that doctrine which set forth the glory of the flesh, which persuaded the wise of the world that life should be spent in delights and pleasure and had deceived the human race by the flattery of luxury — that mouth, I say, is pierced and bored through by the wood of the cross, because that "way" of pleasure which philosophy had proclaimed "broad and spacious," this Christ showed us to be the "narrow and strait way of salvation." Thus, then, Jael the Church delivered over to eternal sleep Sisera the prince of vices, covered with skins — that is, lulled to sleep by the mortification of the members. Yet Jael the Church, after this, also "met" the former people as it pursued Sisera. For Israel "pursued the law of righteousness, but did not attain to the law." The Church, therefore, also "met" that very people and "showed" it its work, showed it the victory accomplished, and invites it into fellowship with the overthrown enemy. For that is true which the Apostle says will come to pass "in the last time": that, "when the fullness of the nations has entered in, then all Israel shall be saved." The "primacy," then, comes to pass indeed "into the hand of" a foreign "woman," yet Barak too is not excluded from the fellowship of glory — Barak who indeed had begun first, but came last to the end. Nay rather, while he arrives, the foreign woman Jael in a manner snatches the passing victory. The same figure went before also in the brothers Esau and Jacob. For while Esau pursues the wild things, while he lingers in the forest glades, Jacob, coming before him and offering to his father the foods of blessing prepared, likewise by the counsels of his mother, received the birthright's blessing. So too in the Gospel, as the Lord was going to raise up "the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue," the "woman who suffered from an issue of blood," coming before, first obtains healing by her faithful touch.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if from this too something seems worthy of being asked by diligent hearers — namely that he is said to have "given him milk to drink" when he had asked for "water" — let us see whether perhaps, according to the mystical or allegorical laws, something of this kind can also be shown concerning this. The food of "milk" is said in the holy Scriptures to be this first moral instruction, which is delivered to beginners as though to "little ones." For at the beginnings the deep and more hidden mysteries are not at once to be delivered to disciples, but the correction of morals, the amendment of discipline, the first elements of religious conduct and of simple faith are delivered to them. This is the "milk" of the Church, these are the first elements of the "little ones" who are beginning. But this food indeed bestows life and salvation upon those who bear the purpose of advancing toward the good; whereas upon those to whom contrary things are pleasing, to whom luxury, lust, avarice, and all impiety are dear, doctrine of this kind furnishes death and destruction. Thus, then, it comes about that from these same foods by which the good are nourished, the evil are choked, and where for the pious there is life, there for the impious there is death. Finally, that the matter of which we speak may become plainer by an example: wine helps the healthy and those living suitably and, as Scripture says, "gladdens the heart of man" — of the healthy man at least — but to the feverish, if they take it, it straightway brings ruin and destruction. So it comes about that the same thing, taken in the same way, confers on one indeed life, but on another death. Thus, then, it is also to be understood that this Sisera, the "animal man" and prince of vices, was extinguished through the doctrine of the Church, which he did not receive in faith. But let each and every soul also strive to lull to sleep and extinguish Sisera within itself by this evangelical and apostolic milk. For if anyone, taught through these things, has "mortified his members which are upon the earth, avarice, fornication" and the rest which the holy Apostle enumerates, he will be seen to have slain Sisera within himself — so that these things may be shown to be accomplished not only in the person of the Church, but also that each one may show them to be fulfilled in his own soul. Since, therefore, as we have said, Sisera indeed began to be pursued by the former people, but was slain by a woman — this Church of the nations — and into her hand was given the palm of victory, at the consummation of all things, that is, at the end of the age, a song too will be sung to the Lord through Deborah, in which the "primacy" will indeed be given to Jael, the Church of the nations, nor yet will Barak's praise be passed over in silence, but one and the same reward of victory will be given to both the first and the last, through Jesus Christ our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The fourth song is in the book of Judges, concerning which it is written: "And Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam sang on that day, saying: When the leaders in Israel began, in the purpose of the people, bless ye the Lord. Hear, O kings, and give ear," and the rest. But she who sings these things ought to be a bee, whose work is such that both kings and ordinary folk use it for health. For Deborah, who sings this song, is interpreted "a bee," and Barak too along with her: and Barak is interpreted "lightning-flash." And this song is sung after victory, because no one can sing what is perfect until he has conquered his adversaries. So, finally, in the song itself it is said: "Arise, arise, Deborah, rouse up the thousands of the people. Arise, arise, sing a song, arise, Barak." But concerning these things too you will find matters more fully discussed in those little discourses which we have published on the book of Judges.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, PROLOGUE

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Sisera, together with his army and his "iron chariots", with which he was assailing the people of God, was overcome, as prophecy had foretold would come to pass through Deborah. And after the victory was accomplished "by the hand of a woman", Deborah is recorded to have sung this song as, so to speak, the very praise of that victory. But if we remember the things that were said in the earlier passages — namely, according to the mystical pattern, what figure Deborah is, and Barak likewise, what image the woman Jael holds, who alone cast down the adversary of God's people, what image Sisera himself is, who was laid low by a foreign woman through the power of wood — we understand that all these are sacraments which are brought to completion in the last times and at the end of the age through the Church, and that in this song is described, as it were, its triumph-song, that is, the praise of the victory, of that time namely when "the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed". For then Deborah shall exult, that is, the glory of prophecy shall be made illustrious, because the things which she foretold have been fulfilled. Then Jael the Church shall overcome the common enemy of all, and, "after the fullness of the nations has entered in", then Barak too, that is, "the remnant of Israel shall be saved" and shall be received into fellowship of the victory. Then therefore, if we have been worthy, we too shall sing this song filled with mystical and prophetic sacraments; and since to examine everything of it point by point is not for the time available — for the hearers of the Church love brevity — yet, discoursing on a few things either of its beginnings or picking out here and there little flowers from it, we shall try to bring some consolation to the hearers, or at least to train and exercise ourselves, that we may be made fit to sing out Deborah's song.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "In the beginning, when the princes were in Israel, in the free wills of the people, bless the Lord". The blessing, he says, with which "we bless the Lord", let it be "in the outset of the princes in Israel", and then afterwards also "in the free wills of the people". For example, when we first begin to come to the worship of God, when we receive the beginning of the word of God and of heavenly teaching, these beginnings must be taken up by us from the "princes of Israel". And by "princes of Israel", that is, of the Christian people, I think we must understand the "angels", whom the Lord says are present to each "least one" in the Church, who are also said "always to see the face of the Father who is in heaven". They therefore are the "princes", and from them our beginnings must be taken. For example, if a boy goes to school, he is indeed received by the master and becomes the pupil of that teacher, but he does not immediately take the outset of his learning from the teacher himself; rather, when he has received from him only the first elements, he is handed over to others to be instructed — to the, so to speak, princes of the school itself; so that, when he has been taught by them, as far as lies in them, and has laid down among them his first rudiments, then at last he may receive also the more perfect precepts of the teacher himself. So therefore even now, recalling the beginnings of our instruction, prophecy says that, when we have begun from the "princes" or the "princes" have begun to work in us, then we should follow on with our own will and purpose, and, increased by our advances, come thus at last to blessing the Lord himself. But see what it says: "in the beginning", it says, "the princes in Israel". It is the "beginnings" that are said to be helped by the "princes"; but after these one must strive by one's own will and purpose, that we may deserve to bless the Lord. For the people of Israel too, when they were beginning to go out from Egypt and to cross the Red Sea, did nothing by their own labor, but everything was done through the princes, that is, through the angels. Indeed, Moses too says thus to the people: "you", he says, "shall keep silence, and the Lord shall fight for you". Or is not the "destroying" angel plainly described as having fought for them — the angel who slew the firstborn of the Egyptians, but of the Israelites did not make even a beast to mutter? But we must not always wait for the angels to "fight for us", but only "in the beginning", that is, in our beginnings, are we helped by the "princes", the angels. For the rest, with the progress of time it behooves us also to go out ourselves, armed for the battles. For before we learn wars, before we practice to fight the battles of the Lord, we are lifted up by the "princes", the angels; before we obtain the provision of "heavenly bread" and are filled with the flesh of the "spotless lamb", before we are made drunk with the blood of the "true vine" which came up from the root of David, so long as we are "little ones" and are nourished with "milk" and hold to the word of the beginnings of Christ, we act, like "little ones", "under guardians and stewards", the angels. But when we have now tasted the sacraments of "the heavenly warfare" and have been refreshed with the "bread of life", hear how we are roused to battle through the apostolic trumpet. For with a mighty voice Paul cries out to us, saying: "put on the armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil". He no longer allows us to lie hidden under the wings of "those who give suck"; he invites us to the fields of combat: "put on", he says, "the breastplate of charity", and "take" likewise "the helmet of salvation", and also "the sword", he says, "of the spirit", and above all "the shield of faith, with which", he says, "you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the evil one". You see, then, how all things are done in order, and nothing confused is carried on among the people of God, nothing disordered or done in reverse. "In the beginning the princes" help; when you have been helped and instructed by the princes, now do for yourself, of your own accord and by your own will, the things you have learned from the princes. For rightly, when the beginnings have been digested and the rudiments laid down, we are committed to our own will, so that either the praise may deservedly be ours, which was gained by our own virtue, or the fault may justly be ours, which came through our own sloth. So much for that which is written: "in the beginning, when the princes were in Israel, in the free wills of the people, bless the Lord".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After this it says: "hear, O kings, and give ear, O satraps: to the Lord I will sing, I will sing praise to the God of Israel". "Hear", it says, "O kings". It calls "kings" those who are summoned to hear the word of God. Exult, O people of God, hearing the insignia of your nobility. You are called to hear the word of God, and you are called not as the common crowd, but as a king. For to you it has been said: "a royal priestly race, a people for acquisition". Therefore, because you are "kings", deservedly is our king Christ the Lord called "king of kings and lord of those who rule". But just as you have exulted over the title of your nobility, so ought you to learn what each of you must do to become a king. Which I will define for you thus, briefly. It makes you a king over all, if Christ reigns in you; for a king is so called from ruling. If therefore in you too the mind reigns and the body obeys, if you send the desires of the flesh under the yoke of your dominion, if you press down the nations of the vices with the tighter reins of your sobriety, deservedly are you called a "king", who have known how to rule yourself rightly. When therefore you have been made such, worthily, as a king, will you be called to hear the divine words. But this which follows indicates something more corporeal, where it says: "give ear, all you satraps". For just as a satrap is lower than a king, so also to give ear seems to be something lower than to hear. For to hear pertains to the inner man, as the Lord too said: "he who has ears to hear, let him hear"; but to give ear regards the outer and bodily hearing. Therefore here too those who ought to "hear" are called "kings", but those who are to "give ear" are called "satraps". "I to the Lord will sing, and I will sing praise to the God of Israel". Blessed are those who are able "to sing a song to the Lord". When we return to the Scriptures, we find many songs committed to the sacred volumes. We have a whole volume written about the Songs of Songs. Behold, in this book of Judges too we have a song, and in Numbers a song is written, and in Deuteronomy, and in Exodus, and in the first book of Kingdoms; in the first book of Chronicles too, and in many other places, you will find that divine songs are recorded. Here therefore the voice of the just man says: "I to the Lord will sing, and I will sing praise to the God of Israel". Who, do you think, is of so tuneful a voice and of a spirit so pure and a mind so sincere, that his singing can delight the divine hearing? He assuredly is the one who has in himself no hoarse sound of sin, who bears nothing of offense on his tongue, nothing of grossness in his spirit — he can rightly say: "I to the Lord will sing, I will sing praise to the God of Israel".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But since we do not undertake to expound the continuation of the song point by point, let us at least, skipping over the sequence of the reading, see what it means where it says: "my heart is toward the things that have been appointed for this Israel". This seems to me to be what it means: my heart and my soul and my sense and my whole mind is bent toward that and looks forward to that "which has been appointed" and which has been prepared "for Israel"; I look forward with my whole mind to that which is to come. For if I bend my mind toward that, all the things that are in this world "I will count as dung, that I may gain Christ", who "has prepared" all those things "which eye has not seen and ear has not heard nor has ascended into the heart of man, for those who love him". "My heart", therefore, it says, "is stretched out toward those things". For I no longer bear a human heart, nor do I think the things I think according to man; but because, according to the Scripture, those "to whom the word of God comes are gods", I too look upon these things not with a human but with a divine mind.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "O mighty ones of the people, bless the Lord, you who have mounted upon beasts of burden". What is it "to have mounted upon a beast of burden"? This body of mine is a "beast of burden"; for it was given for the aid of the soul and for its ministry; but it is I, that is, the inner man, "who have mounted upon" this "beast of burden", to whom it is said that I should "bless the Lord". If therefore you have truly mounted upon the body and have been made superior to bodily desires, and the motions of your body are governed by the bridle of the mind and by the direction of the inner man, it is said of you that you "have mounted upon a beast of burden", that you may "bless the Lord". But what is it that follows? "You who sit upon vehicles", it says, "and shine upon she-asses". What do "shining she-asses" seem to be? For the Scripture says that "those who sit upon vehicles and upon shining she-asses" ought "to bless the Lord". To me, as in places so difficult, something of this sort seems the case: when this beast of burden, that is, my body, has come under the yoke of the word of God, then the "vehicle" of my body will begin "to shine", and this "she-ass", that is, my flesh, will then be said "to shine" when it has been adorned with the splendor of chastity and modesty. And thus it is rightly said that the soul "sitting upon a shining she-ass blesses the Lord" and praises him in the midst of those who rejoice.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "There they shall render acts of righteousness to the Lord". That sacrifice is acceptable to the Lord which is offered to God in righteousness and equity, and therefore it is said: "the just have been strengthened in Israel". Among the other nations, indeed, those who are stronger in bodily might are called "mighty" in battle; but in Israel, those who are more just are themselves called the more powerful in wars, because righteousness, even if it be weak in strength, conquers, whereas unrighteousness, even if it have many and strong defenders, is overcome. So therefore in this nation of ours, that is, in the people of God, either through righteousness we overcome or through unrighteousness we are conquered.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Arise, Deborah, arise and rouse up the ten thousands of the people". When does prophecy "arise"? Assuredly at the coming of Christ, and not only does it itself "arise", but it also "rouses up" the peoples to believe. "Lead captivity captive, O son of Abinoam". "Abinoam" is interpreted as "the answer of the father". His son is Barak. He "will take captivity" from the enemies, who has kept the answers of the heavenly Father.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "O Lord, humble for me those stronger than I". This is the voice of the faithful, who confess simply that their enemies are stronger, against whom is our struggle and battle, because "our battle is not against flesh and blood" — otherwise our adversary would not be stronger — but since "our wrestling is against principalities and powers and against the rulers of the darkness of this world and against the spiritual forces of wickedness", therefore the prophet says: "O Lord, humble for me those stronger than I". For how should this so great force of spirits not be far more powerful than human frailty? But in this God "helps our weakness", in that the Apostle says: "I can do all things in him who strengthens me, Christ". These powers, then, are indeed stronger than we; but again, "Christ", who is in us and "strengthens" us, is stronger than all, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "The land rests" as long as sin rests. But the land is said to be moved—that is, those who dwell in the land—when sins have begun to move and disturb the souls of men. And this is why what the present reading now contains has been written. "And the land rested," it says, "for forty years. And the children of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hands of Midian for seven years. And Midian prevailed over Israel." So then, as long as there was righteousness in the land—that is, in those who dwelt in the land—"the land" is said "to have rested"; but when iniquity increased and "they did evil in the sight of the Lord," then, it says, "the Lord delivered them into the hands of Midian for seven years." Nor are the Midianites said to have prevailed over the people of the Lord as long as the people kept the Lord's precepts. But when it began to neglect the divine commandments, the hand of the enemy became stronger and mightier against it. And against that former people bodily enemies rose up when it had transgressed; but against us, who are called Israel according to the spirit, a spiritual enemy without doubt rises up, and when we neglect the commandments of God, when we despise the precepts of Christ, the hand of demons is made mightier against us, and we too are handed over to our enemies when we are deserted by grace.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us see what befalls those who are handed over for their sins. "And the children of Israel made for themselves," it says, "because of the face of Midian, dens in the mountains and in the caves and in the strongholds; and it came to pass, when a man of Israel had sown, that Midian and Amalek and the sons of the East came up against them; and they came upon them and destroyed all the fruits of the land, until one came to Gaza." These things, indeed, that one suffered who was Israel according to the flesh; he sowed the land, but because he had been handed over for his sins to the enemies rising up against him, instead of crops "he reaped corruption." But as for us, who are named Israel according to the spirit, let us consider what such thing can befall us. There is a time when we sow and the enemies cannot corrupt the seeds that we sow, they cannot lie in wait for our husbandry; but there is also a time when we sow and what we sow is corrupted. Let Paul the Apostle teach us about this difference in sowing. Hear, then, what he himself says: "he who sows," he says, "in the flesh, of the flesh shall reap corruption, and he who sows in the spirit, of the spirit shall reap life eternal." These, then, are they whose seeds the Midianites corrupt, who "sow in the flesh." These are they whose "fruits are destroyed" and perish. But those seeds which "are sown in the spirit" the Midianites cannot corrupt. For the adversary powers cannot ascend to the spiritual fields and defile the fresh-broken ground of the spirit belonging to those who "do not sow upon thorns, but break up for themselves fresh ground." But this too must be added; for I wish to admonish both myself along with you concerning wariness over the seeds and diligence over the spiritual fruits. It frequently happens that someone, toiling much in spiritual work, has produced very many fruits and filled his barns with the crops of righteousness and stored up many good works in the inner chamber of his conscience; but afterward, if he grows negligent and after his labor inclines too readily toward pleasures and self-indulgence, all those seeds of good things and the fruits of holy work will be corrupted under the dominion of lust. For when sin has entered in secretly and taken captive the mind of a man, so that he no longer looks to the commandments of God nor willingly climbs the steep road of virtue, all the things that had before been gathered into the barns of conscience perish. Therefore, then, we must keep the admonition of the holy Scripture which says: "with all watchfulness guard your heart." "The heart must" therefore "be guarded" from every sin, and especially in the time of persecution. For if it should befall someone that at a certain time he gather the fruits of righteousness, seek out the works of the virtues, and cultivate himself with all the most approved disciplines, but in the time of persecution deny the faith, that man has emptied out all his stores, and out of all his goods he is suddenly rendered naked and empty, because the whole labor that was long sought and gathered only with much sweat is suddenly poured out, and, as the prophet says, "all his righteous deeds which he did shall not be remembered." Therefore, then, brothers, let us beseech the Lord, confessing to Him our weakness, that He "hand us not over into the hands of Midian," that He "hand not over to the beasts a soul that confesses to Him," that He hand us not over into the power of those who say: When will the time come that power be given us against the Christians, when will these be handed over into our hands who say that they have or know God? And even if we should be handed over and they receive power over us, let us pray to receive strength from God, that we may be able to endure, that our faith may become brighter amid pressures and tribulations, that through our patience their shamelessness may be overcome, and, as the Lord said, "in our patience we may gain our souls," because "tribulation works patience, and patience proof, and proof hope." For our "proof" extends not only as far as blows, but reaches even to the shedding of blood, because Christ also, whom we follow, poured out His blood for our redemption, that from it we might come forth washed in our own blood. For the baptism of blood alone is what renders us purer than the baptism of water rendered us. And this I do not presume of myself, but Scripture reports it, the Lord saying to His disciples: "I have a baptism to be baptized with, which you know not. And how am I pressed until it be accomplished?" You see, then, that He named the shedding of His blood a "baptism." And if in saying these things I give no offense, I fear that this baptism may be more eminent than that baptism which is handed on through water. For of that one, once received, very few are so blessed as to have been able to keep it unstained even to the end of life; but whoever has been baptized with this baptism can sin no more thereafter. And if it is not rash to venture anything in such matters, we may say that through that baptism past sins are purged, but through this one even future sins are done away. There sins are forgiven, here they are shut out. If God would grant me to be washed in my own blood, to receive a second baptism by death undergone for Christ, I would depart from this world secure, so that "the prince of this world," coming to my soul as it departs from this life, would find nothing—nay rather, he would be lulled to sleep by the shedding of my blood, nor would he dare to accuse in anything a soul washed by its own gore, glorified by its own death, cleansed by its own blood. After this baptism the Midianites would no longer rush in to destroy and lay waste the fruits of the soul. For who could follow the soul of a martyr, which, having passed over all the "powers of the air," stretches toward the heavenly altar? For there the "souls of the martyrs" are said to be placed "beneath the altar" of God, "crying out" day and night, saying: "How long, O Lord, who art just and true, dost Thou not avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?" For there, being placed, they stand in attendance upon the divine sacrifices. But blessed are they who merit these things. Blessed are they whose heart, when they depart from the world, does not tremble on account of sin, whom no dread of transgressions terrifies as they go on to the Lord. Blessed is that soul which, by the gore of blood poured out in martyrdom, casts down the airy throngs of demons that meet it. Blessed is he of whom, as he goes to heaven, the angels speak that prophetic word: "Who is this that comes up from Bozrah?"—that is, who ascends from the flesh to heaven. "Who is this that comes up from Bozrah, the redness of his garments?"—by the "redness of his garments" signifying the gore of blood. Blessed, then, are the souls that so follow Christ as Christ went before them. And therefore, because they so follow, they arrive even at the very altar of God, where the Lord Jesus Christ Himself is, the "high priest of the good things to come," "to whom is glory and power unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Granted, the Midianites have gathered against Israel, they who are interpreted as "outside judgment." Granted, these have gathered against Israel, who are outside the judgment of God and "who have sinned outside the law and will perish outside the law." Granted, Amalek too has gathered, who himself is likewise interpreted as "a people that licks up." Granted, this nation too, earthly and given over to the belly and the gullet, has come to make war — a carnal Israel against the spiritual Israel. But what is this, that even the "sons of the East" are mingled with them and are said to come with them to make war on Israel? For my hearer says to me: if it had been written that the "sons" of the West "gathered with them," I would ask nothing; for you would tell me by the laws of allegory that the sons of the West are the sons of darkness, and that they join themselves to those nations, whether such as are outside the judgment of God or such as, given over to the belly, make war on those who strive to see God with the mind. But now, when it is said that the "sons of the East came with Midian and Amalek," how can these things be fittingly expounded? Let us see, then, whether in passages of Scripture so difficult we can find some sense worthy of the divine pages. Everyone who in any manner takes upon himself the name of Christ becomes a "son" "of the East." For thus it is written of Christ: "behold a man, the East is his name." Everyone, therefore, who takes the name of Christ is said to be a "son" "of the East"; but not always do those who receive the name of Christ also remain in the Church of Christ. If therefore you should see heretics who are indeed reckoned by the name of Christ, yet assail the Church of Christ and bring their arms against the faith of Christ, make war on the people of the Lord, and stir up wars against the catholic faith — do not hesitate to say of these that they are indeed "sons of the East," but that they come with the Midianites and with Amalek to assail the people of God, because together with pagans and with Jews the heretics too persecute the Church of God. And I think that it is these who are designated in the "sons of the East."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "All Midian, therefore," it says, "and Amalek and the sons of the East gathered together and went up and came upon them and pitched their camp in the valley of Jezreel." These, who wish to assail the people of God, "pitch their camp in the valleys," in low and lowly places, "in the valley," it says, "of Jezreel." Now we find that Jezreel is interpreted as "the seed of God." Do you see where the adversaries "pitch their camp"? They did not dare to go there where the "fruits of the Spirit" are seen to have already been born, but where the seed of God still lies, where the fruit has not yet come up. For he who "went out to sow" "sows the word" over every place, but hear the Lord himself saying what the seed of God is wont to suffer: "some," he says, "fell by the wayside, and the birds of heaven come and snatch it away." Which, interpreting in what follows, he himself says: "but those who were sown by the wayside are they who hear the word of God and receive it with joy; but the devil comes and takes away from their heart what was sown." So therefore these too now come to the seed of God and wish to "take it away from the heart of those in whom it was sown," because they find them placed in the valleys and pursuing all that is lowest. For they belong to those who receive the word of God humbly and unworthily and, so to speak, with a Jewish understanding, and therefore the demons are able to "snatch it away from their heart." But he who ascends from the humility of the letter to the heights of the spirit, and, fleeing carnal understanding, pursues among the loftier things those which are of the Spirit of God — from him neither the Midianites nor the Amalekites can snatch anything, nor indeed will the "sons of the East" themselves be able to plunder him, set as he is upon the lofty summit of spiritual understanding.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: They, therefore, "pitch their camp in the valleys." "But the Spirit," it says, "of God strengthened Gideon, and he sounded the trumpet, upon the horn of the trumpet, and called Abiezer after him." The continuity of the exposition, indeed, required a different order, but because we are now speaking not so much to comment on the Scriptures as to console the people concerning those things which have been read, we treat here and there, as they occur, of individual points. "He called," it says, "Abiezer after him," who indeed was nowhere at all. Now "Abiezer" is interpreted as "the help of my father." Therefore Gideon seems to have called upon not some man, but the help of the highest Father. Meanwhile he also sends to summon reinforcements. The peoples come together, and the whole army is gathered to Gideon.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And then," it says, "Gideon said to God: if you save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken, behold, here I am, and I will place a fleece of wool on the threshing-floor; and if indeed dew falls upon the fleece and there is dryness upon all the earth, I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken. And it was done so." Since there are so many and innumerable signs or prodigies which Gideon could have asked from God to confirm God's promise, why did it seem good to him, after the angelic voice and the heavenly promise, to ask of God this so novel a sign? For he says: "I will place a fleece of wool on the threshing-floor, and if there is dew upon the fleece only and dryness upon all the earth, I shall be confident that you will save Israel by my hand." And when Gideon had asked this sign of God, he obtained its fulfillment. But granted, O Gideon, that you have obtained the efficacy of the sign; why do you also take the "fleece of wool" and "wring it out into a basin"? What moved you to do this? But granted that you obtained the first sign, why did you ask that a second sign also be given, in a reversed and altered order? For perhaps someone of those who listen more attentively to what is read says that these things do not seem to agree with what is written: "you shall not tempt the Lord your God," which the law commanded. But the outcome of the matter teaches that nothing was done against the commandment; for neither would God hear a petition demanding something against the law. But now, when we see that in the first sign "dew fell upon the fleece of wool, but on all the earth there was dryness," and in the second "dew fell upon all the earth, but there was dryness in the fleece" — in which Gideon also received confidence that the Lord would by his hand save Israel — the meaning of this mystery must be considered. Concerning it I recall that one also of our predecessors, in his little books, called the "fleece of wool" the people of Israel, and set down the rest of the earth as the rest of the nations, and said that the "dew" which fell "upon the fleece" is the word of God, which had been granted from heaven to that people alone. For upon Israel alone had come the "dew" of the divine legislation; but "dryness" held all the nations, because no moisture of the divine utterance was poured into them. But the meaning of the second sign, altered to the contrary, in which he says: "that upon all the earth the dew should descend, but upon the fleece dryness should remain" — such a meaning is discovered. Behold this whole people which throughout all the earth has been gathered from the nations, now having in itself the divine dew; behold it watered with the dew of Moses, bedewed with the writings of the prophets; behold it growing green also with the moisture of the Gospel and of the apostles; but that fleece, that is, the Jewish people, suffering the dryness and aridity of the word of God, according to what is written: "the children of Israel shall be a long time without a king, without a prince, without a prophet; there shall be no altar nor victim nor sacrifice." You behold how great a "dryness" abides among them, how great an "aridity" of the divine discourse befalls them. These things, indeed, as it is fitting to confess, have been furnished to us from the labor of our elders; but since we too, having heard a word from the wise, as it is written, ought to commend it and add to it, let us see what we too may build up upon such things. For indeed, when I was often examining the seventy-first psalm within myself, this moved me: that, when it describes the coming of Christ in it, in that very psalm it also asserts that this shall come to pass: "and he shall descend," it says, "like rain upon a fleece, and like raindrops dripping upon the earth." A "fleece" is named here, a "fleece" is written also in the psalms. For "he shall descend like rain," it says, "upon a fleece." He "descended," therefore, "upon" that "fleece" of the people of the circumcision, and "like raindrops dripping upon the earth," that is, upon the rest of the earth, "descended" our Lord Jesus Christ, "dripping" also "upon" us and bringing drops of heavenly dew to us also, the nations, that we too might drink, we who were dried up "over" all the "earth" by continual aridity. This order of the mystery, therefore, the holy Gideon, beholding it with prophetic spirit, not only asked the first sign of God, but also repeated a second in reversed order. For he knew that the divine "dew," which is the coming of the Son of God, was to come not only to the Jews, but afterward also to the nations, since indeed from the "unbelief" of Israel "salvation comes to the nations." And this is why, in place of the aridity of the fleece, the whole earth is watered with the grace of the divine dew. But this too, in this deed of the most faithful man Gideon, I think ought by no means to be passed over, since it can serve us as a pattern of spiritual caution. "He saw an angel," but as a learned man, and having now the example of Joshua his predecessor, he acts more cautiously. For he knew that even the angels of darkness could "transfigure themselves into angels of light," and therefore, with most cautious examination, "I wish," he says, "to test the spirit, whether it be from God," because "the spiritual man examines all things." For thus also his predecessor Joshua son of Nun had done; when he had seen "the prince of the heavenly host," he inquires and considers whether he is "ours or of the adversaries." In this manner also the most holy Gideon considers the angelic vision by the diversity and change of the signs.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But that also, which Gideon says: "I will place the fleece" — not just anywhere, not in a field nor in a woodland, but "on the threshing-floor" — how does it seem to you? "On the threshing-floor," where the "harvest" is: "for the harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few." "I will place," he says, "the fleece" there, where the "harvest" is. What had moved the holy man Gideon, or what had seemed good to him, that he should do this? For he foresaw through the Spirit that Christ "gathers" his people "into the threshing-floor" and there cleanses him, "holding the winnowing-fan in his hand," and there separates the "chaff" from the wheat. Not without cause, therefore, did so great and such a man — of whom the holy Apostle too, writing to the Hebrews, makes mention in the catalogue of the prophets — choose the threshing-floor for placing the fleece; nor without cause did he "wring out the fleece into a basin and fill it with water." Let us seek concerning this also in the holy Scriptures, whether any occasion of this understanding too is afforded us. Let us come to the Gospel. We find there our Lord and Savior "putting off his garments, and, girded with a linen cloth, pouring water into a basin, and washing the feet of his disciples." You see, then, that the prophets foreshadowed these things, which were to be fulfilled in the last times through the Lord. That "water," therefore, which "Jesus poured into the basin," was the dew of heavenly grace, with which "he washed the feet of his disciples." Whence also he rightly said to them: "but you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you." But we too, if only we offer our feet, the Lord Jesus is ready to "wash the feet" of our soul and to cleanse them with the heavenly dew, with the grace of the Holy Spirit, with the word of doctrine. For he willed that not the Apostles alone should be "clean," but also all who believe through his word. And to all believers he says that which he said to Peter: "unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me." For it is certain that no one "has part with Christ" unless he has been washed and made "clean." Come, I beseech you, Lord Jesus, Son of God, "put off the garments" which you put on for my sake, and gird yourself for my sake, and "pour water into a basin and wash the feet" of your servants, wash away the filth of your sons and daughters. "Wash the feet" of our soul, that we, imitating you and following you, may "put off" our old "garments" and say: "by night I have put off my garment, how shall I put it on?", and may say again: "I have washed my feet, how shall I soil them?". For as soon as you "wash" my "feet," may you also make me recline with you, that I may hear from you: "you call me Lord and master; and you say rightly, for I am. If therefore I, the Lord and master, have washed your feet, you too wash one another's feet." I too, therefore, now wish to "wash the feet" of my brethren, to "wash the feet" of my fellow-disciples. And for that reason I take the water which I draw from the fountains of Israel, or rather which I "wring out" from the Israelite "fleece." For I now "wring out" water from the "fleece" of the book of Judges, and at another time water from the "fleece" of the Kingdoms, and water from the "fleece" of Isaiah or Jeremiah; and I "pour" it "into the basin" of my soul, conceiving the sense in my heart, and I take the feet of those who offer and prepare themselves for washing, and, so far as I am able, I desire to "wash the feet" of my brethren and to fulfill the commandment of the Lord, that by the word of doctrine the hearers may be cleansed from the filth of their sins, that they may cast away from themselves all the uncleanness of their vices and have clean "feet," with which they may rightly walk "to the preparation of the Gospel of peace," so that all of us together, purified in Christ through the word, may not be cast out from the bridal chamber of the bridegroom on account of filthy garments, but, white in raiment, washed in feet, "clean of heart," may recline at the banquet of the bridegroom, our Lord Jesus Christ himself, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Vast was the multitude that had been gathered against Israel, so great that for its number it was compared to "locusts". "And their camels", it says, "were like the sand which is beyond number upon the shore of the sea". Let us see, then, how so countless a multitude of enemies could be overcome: there went out, it says, thirty-two thousand armed men from the sons of Israel with Gideon to fight against all that multitude. And God gave answer to Gideon, saying: "The multitude that is with you is great". And what if "the multitude is great"? Does not a more numerous army in wars afford safer defenses? By no means, He says, for divine battles are not carried out as human ones are. The work of the divine power is not made illustrious if it is propped up by human supports, because: "a king is not made safe by the greatness of his own power". Therefore, lest perhaps Israel should boast and in its vaunting claim a share of the victory, the Lord says to Gideon: "The people with you are many; I will not deliver Midian into their hands, lest perhaps Israel exult against Me, saying that my own hand has saved me."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Therefore speak in the ears of the people, saying: Whoever is timid and fearful of heart, let him return. And there returned from Mount Gilead, out of the people, twenty-two thousand men, and there remained ten thousand. Let us see, then, first, what it means that He says: "timid and fearful of heart"; for two things are named by which human frailty is convicted, that is, the "timid" and the "fearful" of heart. He may seem "timid" who at the first sight trembles at the encounter, yet is not terrified with his whole heart, but can be restored and heartened again. But the fearful man is he who, the vice as it were now taking root, is terrified by thought alone even before he sees the evils, rolling an icy dread through his limbs, so that he is unmanned not so much by the sight of evils as by the very hearing and expectation of them; and therefore He added: "fearful of heart"; for this vice, now in the "heart", remains fixed even in the inner parts of the soul. What then? Do we say that only at that time did Gideon say to the people: "If anyone is timid and fearful of heart", let him depart from the battles, forsake the wars, abandon the contests of brave men? Or does even today the "commander of our army", our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, cry out to His soldiers and say: "If anyone is timid and fearful of heart", let him not come to My wars? For this is what, in other words indeed but in the same sense, He says in the Gospels: "He who does not take up his cross and follow Me is not worthy of Me", and: "He who does not hate his father and his mother, and his brothers and sisters, and moreover even his own soul, is not worthy of Me", and again: "He who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be My disciple". Does not Christ in these words plainly separate and set apart the "timid and fearful" from His camp? All of you, then, who wish to follow the warfare of Christ, who desire to be in His camp, banish far from you the fear of the mind, banish far the dread of the heart, so that with confidence the soldier of Christ may say: "If camps stand together against me, my heart shall not fear; if battle rise up against me, in this will I hope", and may confidently say: "The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life, of whom shall I tremble?". But do not let such warfare deter you: it contains nothing difficult in itself, nothing arduous or impossible. Do you wish to know how easy it is to fulfill these things for those who wage war out of faith? In these camps even women too are often accustomed to conquer, because the fighting is done not by the strength of the body but by the power of faith. In what went before, in this very little book of Judges, we read of the triumphs of the woman Deborah, and no unbelieving dread disturbed her womanly mind. And why should I recall that magnificent Judith, most noble of all women? who, when affairs were already almost lost, did not tremble to come to the rescue alone, and alone to expose herself and her own head to the slaying of the utterly monstrous Holofernes, and went forth to war relying not on arms nor on war-horses nor on military supports, but on strength of soul and the confidence of faith; by counsel together with daring she destroyed the enemy; and the liberty of the fatherland, which the men had lost, a woman restored. And why do we unroll for you examples of the ancients from so far off? Before our own eyes we have often seen it done, that women and girls still of tender age have borne for the sake of martyrdom the tyrant's torments, to whom, added to the weakness of their sex, was the frailty of their still youthful life. So then, in those who wage war for the truth, and also those who wage war for God, not bodily but spiritual fortitude is required, because the victory is sought not by iron javelins but by the darts of prayers, and it is faith that furnishes endurance in the contest. Whence also the holy Apostle equips the soldiers of God for wars of this kind with fitting arms, saying: "Stand therefore, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, and having girt your loins in truth; but take also the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit; and above all take up the shield of faith, in which you may be able to quench the fiery darts of the wicked one"; but he also bids that the "feet be shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace", and that, armed in this manner, they "take up" the standards "of the cross of Christ and follow Him". Yet this too is permitted in the warfare of Christ, that if perchance at some time you feel yourself inferior in strength amid persecutions, and the contest against the cruelty of the tyrant seems to you unequal through the frailty of the body, you may give place to wrath and "flee" from place to place, nor is this reckoned to you as a soldier's offense. For this too is appointed in the laws of Christ, who says: "If they persecute you in this city, flee into another; and if in the other, flee into yet another". For the sum of the matter is not to deny Jesus, whom you have once confessed. For it is certain that he confesses Him who flees for this reason, that he may not deny Him. If anyone, then, is "timid" and "fearful of heart", let him depart from the camp, let him return to his own house, lest he furnish to the rest an example of fear and dread. But do you wish to see of how great a crime the "timid and fearful" man is guilty? In the Apocalypse, where those are enumerated who are to be cast "into the lake of fire", there before all He places the "timid and fearful", and reckons together with them also the "unbelieving and fornicators and poisoners". Thus among enormous and abominable crimes is placed the crime of fear and dread. And these things we have said on account of those who first, as "timid and fearful of heart", are dismissed from the camp.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But after these "twenty-two thousand departed", the divine discourse adds still further and "says to Gideon": "Still", it says, "the people are many; bring them down to the water, and there I will test them for you". As I see it, those who were first rejected had not even gone down "into the water", but were still marking themselves out as catechumens, and were so deterred by the vice of dread that they did not even go down to the saving washing: those, then, were rejected in this way. But these second ones come "to the water", that they may be tested there. And how they are tested, let us see:

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And the Lord said", it says, "to Gideon: everyone who shall lap the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set him apart; and everyone who shall bend his knees to drink, you shall set him aside. And the number", it says, "of those who lapped the water in their hand or with the tongue was three hundred men, but all the rest bent their knees to drink the water. And the Lord said to Gideon: by these three hundred men who lapped I will save you and deliver Midian into your hand". In almost all the deeds of the ancients vast mysteries are signified, as we see happening also in this passage, because those who go down "to the water", that is, who come to the grace of baptism, ought not to fall down to the earth nor "bend their knees" and yield to the temptations that are to come, but to stand bravely and steadfastly, as the prophet also said: "Lift up the hands that hang down and the loosened knees", and: "Make straight the going of your paths". You have come to the water of baptism; this is the beginning of the contest and of the spiritual battle, from here arises for you the commencement of the fight against the devil. If you are the more slack, if you can easily be made to bend, how will you fight, how will you stand against the wiles of the devil? Therefore the Apostle also cries out: "Stand therefore, and do not again cling to the yoke of bondage", and again he says: "Stand in the Lord", and a third time he says: "For we now live, if you stand in the Lord". That one, then, is approved, that one is chosen, who, after coming to the waters of baptism, knows not how to be bent toward earthly and bodily necessities, who does not indulge the vices nor is laid prostrate through thirst for sin. But as for its saying that they "lapped the water with the hand or the tongue", this seems to me written not without a certain significance of a mystery, namely that the soldiers of Christ ought to work with hand and tongue, that is, by deed and by word, because "he who teaches and does, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven". And that Scripture also set down the likeness of a dog lapping — this animal seems to me to be named in this place for the reason that above all other animals it is said to keep love for its own master, and neither by time nor by injuries is its affection reported to be blotted out in it. Three hundred only, then, who prefigured the image of this mystery, these are the chosen, these the approved, these consecrated to victory, who by the very mystery of the number could prevail over the adversaries. For they are three hundred, who multiply a hundred by three and bear the number of the perfect Trinity, under which number the whole army of Christ is reckoned. Among whom let us wish that we too may deserve to be enrolled.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Yet how do these fight? "Pitchers", it says, they carry, "and lamps and horn trumpets in their hands", and thus, it says, they come against those countless multitudes of the enemy, among whom were "camels like the sand of the sea". And when they had come to the battle, "with the horn trumpets", it says, "they sounded". And they let go the "pitchers" from their hands, and "they were shattered". But then, snatching up the lamps, they rush upon the adversaries, and at the same time crash out with the trumpets. See how the chosen soldiers of God fight with lamps. For thus had Christ armed them, saying: "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning", and again: "So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven". With such lamps kindled, then, it befits the soldiers of Christ to fight, shining with the light of their works and with the splendor of their deeds. But what are the "horn trumpets" on which "they blow the trumpet"? He who speaks of heavenly things, who discourses of spiritual things, who reveals the "mysteries of the kingdom of heaven", he sounds the "trumpet"; he speaks of the "trumpet" who speaks of great and greatest things, who lays open the knowledge of Christ to human ears. But why is the "trumpet" also called "of horn"? Because it is also said of the holy one: "his horn shall be exalted in glory". Whence also each man's "trumpet" is called "of horn" in this, that he discourses the manifold knowledge of Christ and the mysteries of His cross, which is signified in the horn. Warring, then, with this "trumpet", and fighting with this, we overcome the strangers and turn the enemies to flight, even if "their multitude be like locusts". For to "locusts" is compared the multitude of demons, who have a seat neither in heaven nor on the earth. Let there go before us also in this battle the light of works, the power of knowledge, the preaching of the divine word. Let us too fight, singing together in "hymns and psalms and spiritual songs" and "crying out to God", that we may deserve to obtain from Him the victory in Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
The remaining sacrifices, of which those relating to the law are a symbol, are akin to this sacrifice. But in addition, the other sacrifices akin to this sacrifice seem to me to be the shedding of the blood of the noble martyrs. It was not in vain that the disciple John saw them standing beside the heavenly altar. "But who is wise, that he shall understand these things? Or intelligent, and he shall know them?"3Now comprehend, even if to a limited extent, the more spiritual sense of such sacrifices which cleanse those for whom they are offered; one must understand the sense of the sacrifice of the daughter of Jephthah who was offered as a burnt offering because of the vow of him who conquered the children of Ammon. She who was offered as a burnt offering consented to this vow, for, when her father said, "I have opened my mouth to the Lord against you," she said to him, "And if you have opened your mouth to the Lord against me, perform your vow."
Such accounts give an appearance of great cruelty to God to whom such sacrifices are offered for humanity's salvation. We need a generous and perceptive spirit in order to refute the reproaches made against providence and, at the same time, to make a defense of all the sacrifices insofar as they are rather mysterious and beyond human nature.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6.276-78

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The Spirit, therefore, "asks" and "intercedes," but we "pray." And Joshua's words commanding the sun to stand over [Gibeon] seem to me to be an intercession also.… And in Judges, Samson in my opinion said in intercession: "Let me die with the foreigners—when he bent in his strength and the house fell upon the princes and all the people that were there." Even though it is not written that Joshua and Samson "interceded" but that they "said," nevertheless their words seem to be an "intercession," which we must judge to be different from a "prayer," if we are to give words their proper meaning.

author: Pacian of Barcelona
quote: On the name Catholic I answered fully and with calmness. For I said, that it mattered to neither, what the other was called. And if you demanded the meaning of the name, I said that, whatever it might be, it was wonderful, whether it was 'one in all,' or 'one over all,' or (an interpretation which I have not mentioned before,) 'the king's son,' that is, 'the Christian people.' Certainly too that was no accessory name which endured through so many ages. And indeed I am glad for thee that although thou mayest have preferred others, yet thou agreest that the name attaches to us. What, should you deny? Nature would cry out. But and if you still have doubts, let us hold our peace. We will both be that which we shall be named, witness the antiquity of the name. If, however, thou perseverest in asking, beware lest that man of might exclaim, Why askest thou thus after My Name, seeing it is wonderful? I next added, that we need not consider, whence Catholics derived this name, because neither was it wont to be any imputation against the Valentinians, if they were called after Valentinus, nor the Phrygians, if from Phrygia, nor the Novatians, if after Novatian.

author: Paulinus of Nola
quote:
Like the famed Samson, whose power lay in the strength of his hair, whose locks were endowed with sacred might, he must throttle and bring low the lion by means of the strong arms of prayers and pluck the sweet fruit of notable victory from its dead mouth.But this triumph must be a lesson to him not to make alliances with foreigners. That woman of another race I interpret as the law of the flesh, so wily with its alluring nets. If this law proves stronger than the law of the mind, it will drag him into the dominion of sin. The evil counsel of its pleasant words weakens with its deceitful guile the male spirit. It blinds the eyes of the mind and shaves the head; it plunders and disarms faith. I would not have our boy a Samson in this respect, becoming involved in a love encounter immediately followed by captivity, enervation and blindness, even though the strong Samson later recovered his strength when his hair grew again. For he was led by the hand from the mill to be the sport of the vaunting enemy, and though physically blind he used his mind's eye and summoned God to take vengeance. Then, when his hair restored his strength, he brought down that house of the enemy. Once his hands, more powerful than any stone, gripped the pillars of the house in their fierce embrace, the roof collapsed upon him when its props were torn from the earth. Yet even in his death God's powerful hero involved the foe in destruction, and by a glorious death [he] avenged the disgrace of his life as a slave. He had lived a life of subservience under an exultant foe, but even as he fell he conquered the eclipsed enemy, destroying more thousands at his death than he had killed in his life.
I pray that our son may imitate Samson's death by his own, that while remaining in the flesh he may conquer that flesh and live for God, subduing the sins of the flesh. I would not have him devoting his heart in enslavement to the flesh's joys as to the wiles of that criminal woman, to become subsequently the property of the foe, stripped of the strength of grace.

author: Procopius of Gaza
quote: "Awake, Awake, Deborah!" Increase righteousness, establish the people, arise for the glory of God and the salvation of the people. "Gathering strength, arise Barak!" Arise and establish [the people] as was said to Moses, "Stand by me." David likewise said, "Our feet stand in your courts, O Jerusalem." "He set my feet upon the rock." Therefore, gathering strength, arise and say, "I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me!" "You are my strength and my song, O Lord." But also you, Deborah, strengthen Barak. For the saints also give courage to us in the power of the Lord, instructing our souls against our enemies. But every mind should be held captive to the obedience of Christ. And if, Deborah, you should fall in your work, like what happened to Jonathan [when he tasted the honey], may your soul be strengthened by the sweet taste of prophecy.

author: Prudentius
quote:
Samson resistless because of his hair is attacked by a lion;
When he killed the wild beast, from its mouth there flowed streams of honey,
And from an ass's jawbone comes forth a fountain of water:
Folly with water overflows and virtue with sweetness.
Samson catches three hundred foxes and arms them with firebrands,
Which he ties to their tails, and he lets them go into the cornfields
Of the Philistines to burn their crops: thus the fox of false doctrine
Cunningly scatters the flames of heresy over our vineyards.

author: Salvian the Presbyter
quote: We read that when God wished it clearly understood that great deeds were done by him, they were done through a few or through the lowliest, lest the work of his heavenly hand be attributed to human strength. In this way the leader Sisera, before whom the Hebrew army trembled, was laid low by a woman.

author: Salvian the Presbyter
quote:
Against the Midianites, also, who, as the book of Judges relates, had filled all places like locusts, Gideon was ordered to lead a few men into battle. It was not that he did not have many in his army, but that he was forbidden to lead many into battle, lest the multitude might claim for itself some share of the victory. Hence, when he had gathered thirty thousand armed fighters, the Lord spoke thus to him: "the people with you are too many, and the Midianites shall not be given into their hands."What happened next? He left only three hundred fighters to the man who was about to fight against countless thousands of barbarians. Indeed, he ordered the line of soldiers to be reduced to the smallest number in order that their fewness would not permit them to realize any credit from the prosecution of the divinely waged war. Why the Lord acted thus, he himself very clearly stated, saying, "lest Israel glory against me and say, 'I am saved by my own strength.' " Let them hear, I say, let all the unjust and the presumptuous hear. Let all the powerful hear what God says when he says, "Lest Israel glory against me and say, 'I am saved by my own strength.' "
I say, let them hear, all those who hurl blasphemies and statements contrary to the above, let them who place their hope in human beings hear these things. God says that all who presume they can be liberated by their own strength speak against him.

author: Tertullian
quote: After the death of Joshua the son of Nave [Nun] they forsook the God of their fathers and served idols, Baalim and Ashtaroth; and the Lord in anger delivered them up to the hands of plunderers, and they continued to be plundered by them and to be sold to their adversaries, and [they] could not at all stand before their enemies. Wherever they went forth, his hand was upon them for evil, and they were greatly distressed. And after this God sets judges, the same as our censors, over them. But not even these did they continue steadfastly to obey. So soon as one of the judges died, they proceeded to transgress more than their fathers had done by going after the gods of others and serving and worshiping them. Therefore the Lord was angry. "Since, indeed," he says, "this nation has transgressed my covenant which I established with their fathers and has not hearkened to my voice, I will not remove from them any of the nations which Joshua left at his death." And thus, throughout almost all the annals of the judges and of the kings who succeeded them, while the strength of the surrounding nations was preserved, he meted wrath out to Israel by war and captivity and a foreign yoke, as often as they turned aside from him, especially to idolatry.
